# Agent Overview

The Agent is the foundation of Promptise Foundry. `build_agent()` returns a production-ready agent with opt-in capabilities: memory, guardrails, semantic cache, reasoning patterns, approval workflows, streaming, and more. Every feature is one parameter away.

## Quick example

```python
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent, StdioServerSpec

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={
            "math": StdioServerSpec(
                command="python",
                args=["-m", "my_math_server"],
            ),
        },
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 42 * 17?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

asyncio.run(main())
```

!!! info "You need an API key first"
    Every model provider needs a credential. Put it in a `.env` file in your project (Promptise loads it automatically, in scripts and in the CLI) or pass it in code with `Model(...)`, explained in [**Models & Providers → In code: Model**](../core/agents/models.md#in-code-model): `Model("gpt-5-mini", provider="openai", api_key="...")`. The **exact variable name for every provider** (Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Gemini, Ollama, …) is in [**Configuration & Secrets → Every provider's variables**](../getting-started/configuration.md#every-providers-variables); self-hosted and inference endpoints are in [**Models & Providers → Custom, self-hosted and inference endpoints**](../core/agents/models.md#custom-self-hosted-and-inference-endpoints). `promptise models env <provider>` prints the lines a provider needs and `promptise models check <model>` tells you what is still missing.

## Capability Map

Every capability is a single parameter on `build_agent()`. Start with just `model` + `servers`, then add capabilities as needed.

```
build_agent()
│
├─ Core
│   model ─────────────── "openai:gpt-5-mini", Model(...), FallbackChain([...]) or a chat model
│   servers ───────────── MCP tool servers (StdioServerSpec, HTTPServerSpec)
│   extra_tools ───────── Your own Python functions as tools (@tool)
│   instructions ──────── System prompt (a string or a Prompt)
│   identity ──────────── AgentIdentity: who the agent is
│
├─ Reasoning ──────────── How does the agent think?
│   agent_pattern ─────── "react", "verify", "managed", "code-action", "peoatr", "research", "autonomous", "deliberate", "debate", or a PromptGraph
│   node_pool ─────────── Reasoning nodes the agent picks from (autonomous graph)
│   max_agent_iterations, context_compaction, context_engine, tool_summary
│
├─ Memory & State ─────── What does the agent remember?
│   memory ────────────── InMemoryProvider, ChromaProvider, Mem0Provider
│   conversation_store ── InMemory/SQLite/Postgres/RedisConversationStore
│   cache ─────────────── SemanticCache (in-memory or Redis)
│   flow ──────────────── ConversationFlow (the system prompt changes per phase)
│
├─ Security & Safety ──── What protects the agent and its users?
│   guardrails ────────── PromptiseSecurityScanner (injection, PII, credentials, ...)
│   approval ──────────── ApprovalPolicy (human-in-the-loop for tool calls)
│   sandbox ───────────── True, a dict or a SandboxConfig (Docker isolation for code)
│
├─ Performance ────────── How fast and cost-effective?
│   optimize_tools ────── "minimal", "standard", "semantic" or a ToolOptimizationConfig
│   adaptive ──────────── True or an AdaptiveStrategyConfig (learn from failed tool calls)
│
├─ Delegation ─────────── cross_agents, include_broadcast, max_delegation_depth
│
└─ Execution ──────────── How do you watch it run?
    observe ───────────── True or an ObservabilityConfig (4 levels, 8 transporters)
    events ────────────── EventNotifier (webhooks and other sinks)
    on_tool_progress ──── Callback for MCP tool progress

Per call: ainvoke(..., caller=CallerContext(...)), chat(...), astream_with_tools(...)
```

## Which Feature Do I Need?

| I want to... | Use this |
|---|---|
| Connect to MCP tool servers | `servers=` with `StdioServerSpec` or `HTTPServerSpec` |
| Give the agent my own Python functions | `extra_tools=` with `@tool`: see [Tools](tools.md) |
| Change how the agent reasons | `agent_pattern=`: see [Reasoning Patterns](agents/reasoning-patterns.md) |
| Give the agent memory across sessions | `memory=`: see [Memory](memory.md) |
| Persist conversations | `conversation_store=`: see [Conversations](conversations.md) |
| Block prompt injection / PII leaks | `guardrails=`: see [Guardrails](guardrails.md) |
| Require human approval for actions | `approval=`: see [Approval](approval.md) |
| Run untrusted code safely | `sandbox=`: see [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| Reduce token costs | `optimize_tools=`: see [Tool Optimization](tool-optimization.md) |
| Cache similar queries | `cache=`: see [Semantic Cache](cache.md) |
| Handle LLM provider outages | `model=FallbackChain([...])`: see [Model Fallback](fallback.md) |
| Stream responses in real-time | `agent.astream_with_tools()`: see [Streaming](streaming.md) |
| Track token usage and latency | `observe=`: see [Observability](observability.md) |
| Multi-user access control | `caller=CallerContext(...)` on each call: see [CallerContext](agents/building-agents.md#callercontext-per-request-identity) |
| Delegate to other agents | `cross_agents=`: see [Cross-Agent Delegation](agents/cross-agent.md) |
| Get notified of errors and blocks | `events=`: see [Events](events.md) |
| Define the agent in YAML | a `.superagent` file: see [SuperAgent Files](agents/superagent-files.md) |

## How Core Modules Relate

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[config.py<br>StdioServerSpec / HTTPServerSpec] -->|feeds| B[tools.py<br>ToolInfo / schema conversion]
    C[types.py<br>ModelLike / ServerSpec] -->|re-exports| A
    D[env_resolver.py<br>resolve env vars] -->|resolves| A
    E[prompt.py<br>DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT] -->|used by| F[agent.py<br>build_agent]
    B -->|provides tools to| F
    G[callback_handler.py<br>PromptiseCallbackHandler] -->|observes| F
    H[exceptions.py<br>SuperAgentError tree] -->|raised by| D
    H -->|raised by| B
    C -->|imported by| F
```

## Module Reference

| Module | Purpose | Key Exports |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| [Config & Server Specs](config.md) | Define how to connect to MCP servers (stdio or HTTP) | `StdioServerSpec`, `HTTPServerSpec`, `servers_to_mcp_config` |
| [Types & ModelLike](types.md) | Central type aliases used across the framework | `ModelLike`, `ServerSpec`, `CrossAgent` |
| [Environment Resolver](env-resolver.md) | Resolve `${VAR}` placeholders in configuration | `resolve_env_var`, `resolve_env_in_dict` |
| [Exceptions](exceptions.md) | Custom error hierarchy for configuration and runtime errors | `SuperAgentError`, `SuperAgentValidationError` |
| [Default System Prompt](default-prompt.md) | The default instructions given to every agent | `DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT` |
| [Callback Handler](callback-handler.md) | Bridge LangChain events into the observability pipeline | `PromptiseCallbackHandler` |
| [Tools](tools.md) | Declare Python functions as tools with `@tool`; convert MCP tool schemas to LangChain tools | `tool`, `ToolError`, `ToolInfo`, `MCPClientError` |

# Building Agents

Create intelligent agents that connect to MCP servers, discover tools automatically, and execute tasks with full observability.

## Quick Example

```python
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        servers={
            "weather": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp"),
        },
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    )

    result = await agent.ainvoke({
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Zurich?"}]
    })
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())
```

!!! info "You need an API key first"
    Every model provider needs a credential. Put it in a `.env` file in your project (Promptise loads it automatically, in scripts and in the CLI) or pass it in code with `Model(...)`, explained in [**Models & Providers → In code: Model**](../../core/agents/models.md#in-code-model): `Model("gpt-5-mini", provider="openai", api_key="...")`. The **exact variable name for every provider** (Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Gemini, Ollama, …) is in [**Configuration & Secrets → Every provider's variables**](../../getting-started/configuration.md#every-providers-variables); self-hosted and inference endpoints are in [**Models & Providers → Custom, self-hosted and inference endpoints**](../../core/agents/models.md#custom-self-hosted-and-inference-endpoints). `promptise models env <provider>` prints the lines a provider needs and `promptise models check <model>` tells you what is still missing.

## Concepts

Promptise agents are built around three ideas:

1. **MCP-first tool discovery**: You point the agent at one or more MCP servers via the `servers` dict. On startup it connects to every server, lists all available tools, and converts them into LangChain-compatible tools automatically.
2. **Opt-in capabilities**: Observability, memory, sandbox execution, cross-agent delegation, and prompt flows are all disabled by default. Enable each one with a single parameter and the agent wires everything together.
3. **Unified return type**: `build_agent()` always returns a `PromptiseAgent`. It wraps the reasoning graph engine (a ReAct tool loop unless you choose another `agent_pattern`) and exposes the same interface whichever capabilities are active.

## Walkthrough

### The `build_agent()` Function

`build_agent()` is the primary entry point for creating agents. It is an `async` function that connects to MCP servers, discovers tools, and returns a ready-to-use agent.

```python
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import StdioServerSpec, HTTPServerSpec

agent = await build_agent(
    # Required -----------------------------------------------
    servers={
        "files": StdioServerSpec(command="python", args=["-m", "file_server"]),
        "api":   HTTPServerSpec(url="https://api.example.com/mcp"),
    },
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",

    # Optional -----------------------------------------------
    instructions="You are a helpful data analyst.",
    trace_tools=True,                   # print every tool call to stdout
    observe=True,                       # enable observability
    memory=None,                        # MemoryProvider instance
    memory_auto_store=False,            # auto-persist exchanges
    sandbox=True,                       # sandboxed code execution
    observer=None,                      # shared ObservabilityCollector
    observer_agent_id=None,             # agent id for shared observer
    cross_agents=None,                  # peer agents for delegation
    extra_tools=[],                     # @tool functions, plain functions, LangChain tools
    flow=None,                          # ConversationFlow for multi-turn prompts
)
```

#### Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `servers` | `Mapping[str, ServerSpec] \| None` | `None` | Named MCP server connections. Leave it out for an agent without MCP tools. See [Server Configuration](server-specs.md). |
| `model` | `str \| Model \| BaseChatModel \| Runnable` | **required** | A provider string (e.g. `"openai:gpt-5-mini"`), a `Model(...)`, a `FallbackChain`, a chat model instance, or any Runnable. See [Models & Providers](models.md). |
| `instructions` | `str \| Prompt \| PromptSuite \| None` | `None` (the [default prompt](../default-prompt.md)) | System prompt. Accepts a plain string, a `Prompt`, or a `PromptSuite`. |
| `identity` | `AgentIdentity \| None` | `None` | Who the agent is. Its id is recorded on every tool call and LLM turn; a verifiable identity (Entra, AWS, GCP, SPIFFE, OIDC) also presents a signed credential to HTTP/SSE MCP servers that have no bearer of their own. See [Agent Identity](../../identity/overview.md). |
| `trace_tools` | `bool` | `False` | Print each tool invocation and result to stdout. Covers MCP, cross-agent, sandbox and `extra_tools` tools, and calls answered from an earlier result (`ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...)`), printed as reused. |
| `observe` | `bool \| ObservabilityConfig \| dict \| None` | `None` | Enable observability. `True` records at the `standard` level and writes an HTML report to `./reports` at shutdown; pass an `ObservabilityConfig` (or a dict of its fields) for full control. |
| `memory` | `MemoryProvider \| dict \| None` | `None` | Memory backend. Automatically searches and injects relevant context before each invocation. |
| `memory_auto_store` | `bool` | `False` | When `True`, automatically stores each user/assistant exchange in memory. |
| `memory_max_results` | `int` | `5` | Most memories injected per invocation. |
| `memory_min_score` | `float` | `0.0` | Drop search results scoring below this relevance (0.0 to 1.0). |
| `memory_timeout` | `float` | `5.0` | Seconds to wait for the memory search (the agent then answers without memory context) and for an auto-store write. Raise it for providers that are slow to start. |
| `sandbox` | `bool \| dict \| SandboxConfig \| None` | `None` | Enable sandboxed code execution. `True` uses defaults; a dict provides custom config (unknown keys raise; the network is `"none"` unless set). Raises if the sandbox cannot be started. See [Sandbox](../sandbox.md). |
| `code_action` | `dict \| CodeActionConfig \| None` | `None` | Only with `agent_pattern="code-action"`: `exec_timeout` (default 120), `max_repairs` (default 1), `max_tool_calls` (default 50, the cap on each program's tool calls, failed ones included; a program that reaches it fails, and a repaired program gets a fresh budget; a job that cannot fit raises `CodeActionBudgetError`). |
| `observer` | `Any \| None` | `None` | Pass an existing `ObservabilityCollector` to reuse across multiple agents. Mutually exclusive with `observe`. |
| `observer_agent_id` | `str \| None` | `None` | Agent identifier for the shared observer's timeline entries. |
| `cross_agents` | `Mapping[str, CrossAgent] \| None` | `None` | Peer agents exposed as `ask_agent_<name>` tools. See [Cross-Agent Delegation](cross-agent.md). |
| `include_broadcast` | `bool` | `False` | Also add a `broadcast_to_agents` tool that asks several peers the same question in parallel. |
| `max_delegation_depth` | `int` | `3` | Most nested delegations one request may make (this agent, peer, peer...). A deeper call is refused with a `DelegationError` the model sees. |
| `delegation_timeout` | `float \| None` | `None` | Seconds to wait for a peer whose `CrossAgent` sets no `timeout`. |
| `expose_resources` | `bool` | `False` | Give the agent the MCP servers' resources: adds `read_resource` (its description lists the resources and URI templates) and `list_resources`. |
| `expose_prompts` | `bool` | `False` | Give the agent the MCP servers' prompts: adds `get_prompt` (its description lists the prompts and their arguments), which returns the rendered prompt for the agent to follow. Like MCP tool calls, both send the invoking caller's bearer token to servers with `forward_caller_token` (the default), so the server's roles and guards judge the user, not the agent. |
| `extra_tools` | `Sequence[BaseTool \| Callable] \| None` | `None` | Your own tools, next to the MCP-discovered ones: functions decorated with `@tool` (`from promptise import tool`), plain functions (made tools as if decorated), and LangChain tools. Anything else raises `TypeError` before any server is connected. See [Your own tools](#your-own-tools-extra_tools). |
| `flow` | `ConversationFlow \| type \| Callable \| None` | `None` | A conversation flow that evolves the system prompt across turns: an instance (used as a template), a subclass, or a factory. Each session or caller gets its own copy. See [ConversationFlow](../../prompting/flows.md#integration-with-build_agent). |
| `guardrails` | `PromptiseSecurityScanner \| bool \| None` | `None` | Security scanner for input/output. `True` uses `PromptiseSecurityScanner.default()`. Blocks injection attacks, redacts PII and credentials. See [Guardrails](../guardrails.md). |
| `optimize_tools` | `bool \| str \| ToolOptimizationConfig \| None` | `None` | Shorter tool definitions, or semantic tool selection. `True` or `"minimal"`, `"standard"`, `"semantic"`, or a `ToolOptimizationConfig`. See [Tool Optimization](../tool-optimization.md). |
| `conversation_store` | `ConversationStore \| None` | `None` | Persistent conversation history. See [Conversations](../conversations.md). |
| `conversation_max_messages` | `int` | `0` | Max messages to retain per session (0 = unlimited). |
| `cache` | `SemanticCache \| None` | `None` | Semantic response cache. Serves similar queries from the cache instead of the model. See [Cache](../cache.md). |
| `approval` | `ApprovalPolicy \| ApprovalHandler \| Callable \| None` | `None` | Human-in-the-loop approval. An `ApprovalPolicy` gates the agent's own matching tool calls; any of the three also answers server-side approval gates that ask the client through MCP elicitation. See [Approval](../approval.md). It also answers the `HumanNode` steps of the agent's graph; without it a `HumanNode` fails the run. |
| `events` | `EventNotifier \| None` | `None` | Webhook/event notifications. Emits structured events on invocation, tool, guardrail, budget, and process events. See [Events](../events.md). |
| `on_tool_progress` | `Callable \| None` | `None` | Called as `(tool_name, progress, total, message)` for each progress notification an MCP tool sends during a call; sync or async. Progress is also emitted as `tool.progress` events when `events` is set. See [Progress Reporting](../../mcp/server/resilience-patterns.md#receiving-progress-in-a-promptise-client-or-agent). |
| `max_invocation_time` | `float` | `0` | Maximum seconds per invocation of `ainvoke()`, `chat()`, `invoke()`, `astream()` and `astream_with_tools()`. A stream's time runs from its first step to its last event, the consumer's time between events included. When exceeded the run (or stream) stops, `TimeoutError("Agent invocation exceeded Ns timeout")` is raised and an `invocation.timeout` event is emitted. A `TimeoutError` raised inside the run (a guardrail, the model client) is reported as that error, not as the invocation timeout. `0` = unlimited. |
| `agent_pattern` | `str \| PromptGraph \| None` | `None` (`"react"`) | The reasoning graph: `"react"`, `"verify"`, `"managed"`, `"code-action"`, `"peoatr"`, `"research"`, `"autonomous"`, `"deliberate"`, `"debate"`, or your own `PromptGraph`. An unknown name raises `ValueError`. See [Reasoning Patterns](reasoning-patterns.md). |
| `pattern` | `str \| PromptGraph \| None` | `None` | Deprecated alias of `agent_pattern`. |
| `node_pool` | `list[BaseNode] \| None` | `None` | Build an autonomous graph from these nodes (the agent picks the next node each step). Takes precedence over `agent_pattern`. |
| `graph_blocks` | `list \| None` | `None` | Prompt blocks added ahead of each prompt node's own blocks: in a built-in pattern given by name, in the default ReAct graph (no `agent_pattern`) and in the `node_pool` nodes (copied, not changed). A `PromptGraph` passed as `agent_pattern` keeps its nodes as they are. Before 1.7.0 the default graph and `node_pool` did not get them. |
| `max_agent_iterations` | `int` | `25` | Most node executions per run. With the default ReAct graph (and `"react"` / `"managed"`), `N` allows at most `N` model calls. A run that stops after the model asked for tools raises `GraphIterationLimitError`. |
| `tool_summary` | `str` | `"off"` | Also list the tools in the system prompt: `"off"`, `"names"` or `"full"` (parameters and the start of each description). |
| `context_engine` | `ContextEngine \| None` | `None` | Token-budgeted assembly of the system prompt layers. See [Context Engine](../context-engine.md). |
| `context_compaction` | `bool \| int \| ContextCompaction \| None` | `None` | How long tool loops are compacted: `None`/`True` compact after 6 tool results, an `int` after that many, `False` never. See [Context Lifecycle](../../guides/context-lifecycle.md). |
| `adaptive` | `bool \| AdaptiveStrategyConfig \| dict \| None` | `None` | Learn from failed tool calls. Needs `memory`. See [Adaptive Strategy](../adaptive-strategy.md). |

### Your own tools: `extra_tools`

Give the agent Python functions as tools with `@tool`.  The name, description
and parameter schema come from the function's name, docstring and type hints,
arguments are validated before the function runs, and a `CallerContext`
parameter receives the caller of the current invocation:

```python
from promptise import CallerContext, ToolError, build_agent, tool
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec


@tool
async def get_order(order_id: str, caller: CallerContext) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, for example "A-1001".
    """
    order = await orders.get(order_id, owner=caller.user_id)
    if order is None:
        raise ToolError(f"No order {order_id}.")
    return order


agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"crm": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    extra_tools=[get_order],
)
```

`ToolError` sends the model an error it can act on; the dict is sent as JSON.
See [Tools](../tools.md#declare-tools-with-tool) for parameter descriptions,
validation, results, timeouts and testing.

### The `PromptiseAgent` Class

`build_agent()` returns a `PromptiseAgent`. This is the unified agent object with opt-in capabilities: disabled features no-op or return sensible defaults, so you never need to check what is active.

#### Members at a glance

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `await ainvoke(input, config=None, *, caller=None, session_id=None)` | Run once. `input` is `{"messages": [...]}`; returns the final state, whose `["messages"][-1]` is the answer. |
| `invoke(...)` | The same, blocking (for scripts without an event loop). |
| `astream(input, *, caller=None)` | Async iterator of `{"messages": [...]}` after each graph step. |
| `astream_with_tools(input, *, caller=None, include_arguments=True, tool_display_names=None)` | Async iterator of chat-UI events: `tool_start`, `tool_end`, `token`, `done`, `error`. See [Streaming](../streaming.md). |
| `await chat(message, *, session_id, user_id=None, caller=None, metadata=None, system_prompt=None)` | Load the session's history from the `conversation_store`, run, store the new messages, return the answer text. Enforces session ownership. See [Conversations](../conversations.md). |
| `await list_sessions(*, user_id=None, limit=50, offset=0)` | Sessions in the store, optionally one user's. |
| `await get_session(session_id, *, user_id=None)` | One session's metadata; checks ownership. |
| `await update_session(session_id, *, calling_user_id=None, user_id=..., title=..., metadata=...)` | Change a session's title, owner or metadata; checks ownership. |
| `await delete_session(session_id, *, user_id=None)` | Delete a session and its messages; checks ownership. |
| `get_flow(session_id=None, *, caller=None, user_id=None)` | The `ConversationFlow` kept for a session or caller (with `flow=`). |
| `get_stats()` | Observability totals (empty dict without `observe`). |
| `generate_report(path, title=...)` | Write the HTML report; raises `RuntimeError` without `observe`. |
| `tools`, `tool_names` | Every tool the agent can call, and their names. |
| `identity` | The `AgentIdentity` passed to `build_agent`, or `None`. |
| `adaptive_strategy` | The `AdaptiveStrategyManager` (with `adaptive=`), or `None`. |
| `collector` | The `ObservabilityCollector` (with `observe=`), or `None`. |
| `last_report` | The engine's `ExecutionReport` for the most recent run: iterations, nodes visited, tool calls, tokens, duration and error. See [ExecutionReport](../engine-hooks.md#executionreport). |
| `await shutdown()` | Close MCP connections, stores and notifiers; flush transporters. |

#### Invocation Methods

```python
# Async invocation (recommended)
result = await agent.ainvoke({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize sales.csv"}]
})

# Async streaming: the conversation after each step of the agent's graph
async for chunk in agent.astream({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain quantum computing"}]
}):
    print(chunk["messages"][-1])  # the last chunk is what ainvoke() returns

# Synchronous invocation (convenience wrapper)
result = agent.invoke({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
})
```

`astream()` yields `{"messages": [...]}` once per step (a model call and the
tools it asked for), applying input and output guardrails, memory and
observability as `ainvoke()` does. For token-by-token text and tool activity,
what a chat UI needs: use [`astream_with_tools()`](../streaming.md).

!!! warning "Sync invocation and memory"
    `invoke()` delegates to `ainvoke()` internally when memory is enabled because memory search requires async I/O. If a running event loop is already active (e.g. inside Jupyter), memory injection is skipped for the sync path. Use `ainvoke()` in async contexts to ensure memory always works.

#### Observability Methods

When `observe=True` is passed to `build_agent()`, the agent records every LLM turn, tool call, and token count.

```python
agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", observe=True
)

result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]})

# Retrieve aggregate statistics
stats = agent.get_stats()
print(stats)

# Generate an interactive HTML report
report_path = agent.generate_report("report.html", title="My Agent Report")
```

`get_stats()` returns an empty dict when observability is disabled. `generate_report()` raises `RuntimeError` if observability is not enabled.

#### Programmatic Metrics

When `observe=True`, the agent internally creates a `PromptiseCallbackHandler` that captures all LLM and tool events. Use `get_stats()` to access aggregate metrics:

```python
agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", observe=True
)

result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]})

stats = agent.get_stats()
stats["total_tokens"]           # Total tokens used (prompt + completion)
stats["total_prompt_tokens"]    # Total input tokens
stats["total_completion_tokens"] # Total output tokens
stats["llm_call_count"]         # Number of LLM calls
stats["tool_call_count"]        # Number of tool calls
stats["error_count"]            # Number of errors
stats["retry_count"]            # Number of retries
```

See [Observability](../observability.md) for full details on the callback handler, transporter configuration, and HTML report generation.

#### Lifecycle: `shutdown()`

Always call `shutdown()` when the agent is no longer needed. It closes MCP connections, flushes observability transporters, and releases the memory provider.

```python
try:
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [...]})
finally:
    await agent.shutdown()
```

`shutdown()` is always safe to call: it no-ops for features that are not enabled.

### Combining Capabilities

Capabilities compose naturally. Here is an agent with observability, memory, and cross-agent delegation all enabled at once:

```python
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec
from promptise.cross_agent import CrossAgent
from promptise.memory import InMemoryProvider

# Build a peer agent first
researcher = await build_agent(
    servers={"search": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8001/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
)

# Build the main agent with all capabilities
agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"files": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8002/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    observe=True,
    memory=InMemoryProvider(),
    memory_auto_store=True,
    cross_agents={
        "researcher": CrossAgent(agent=researcher, description="Web research"),
    },
)

result = await agent.ainvoke({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Research and summarize recent AI papers"}]
})
await agent.shutdown()
await researcher.shutdown()
```

### Security Guardrails

Protect your agent from prompt injection attacks on input and PII/credential leakage on output. The `guardrails` parameter accepts a `PromptiseSecurityScanner`: a composable scanner built from detection heads.

#### Basic: block injections, redact PII and credentials

```python
from promptise import build_agent, PromptiseSecurityScanner

scanner = PromptiseSecurityScanner.default()
scanner.warmup()  # Pre-load models at startup, not on first message

agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", guardrails=scanner,
)
```

With this configuration:

- **Input**: Prompt injection attempts are blocked before reaching the LLM. `GuardrailViolation` is raised.
- **Output**: Credit card numbers, SSNs, API keys, and other sensitive data are replaced with labels like `[CREDIT_CARD_VISA]`, `[AWS_ACCESS_KEY]`.

#### Custom: pick specific detectors

```python
from promptise import (
    PromptiseSecurityScanner,
    InjectionDetector, PIIDetector, CredentialDetector, CustomRule,
    PIICategory, CredentialCategory,
)

scanner = PromptiseSecurityScanner(
    detectors=[
        InjectionDetector(threshold=0.9),
        PIIDetector(categories={PIICategory.CREDIT_CARDS, PIICategory.SSN, PIICategory.EMAIL}),
        CredentialDetector(categories={CredentialCategory.AWS, CredentialCategory.OPENAI}),
    ],
    custom_rules=[
        CustomRule(name="internal_id", pattern=r"EMP-\d{6}", description="Employee ID"),
    ],
)

agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", guardrails=scanner,
)
```

#### Handling blocked input

```python
from promptise.guardrails import GuardrailViolation

try:
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]})
except GuardrailViolation as v:
    print(f"Blocked: {v.report.blocked[0].description}")
```

See [Guardrails](../guardrails.md) for the full reference: all 6 detector types, 165+ built-in patterns, model configuration, air-gapped deployments, and content safety classification.

---

## CallerContext: Per-Request Identity

Every `ainvoke()` and `chat()` call can carry a `CallerContext` that identifies the user making the request. This is the foundation for multi-user systems.

```python
from promptise.agent import CallerContext

caller = CallerContext(
    user_id="user-alice-001",           # Scopes memory, cache, conversations
    tenant_id="acme",                   # Tenant-qualifies ALL isolation keys (multi-tenant SaaS)
    bearer_token="eyJhbGciOi...",       # Sent to HTTP MCP servers on this invocation's tool calls
    roles={"analyst", "viewer"},         # Agent-side role info
    scopes={"read", "write"},            # Agent-side scope info
    metadata={"team": "finance"},        # Custom metadata
)

result = await agent.ainvoke(input, caller=caller)
```

### What CallerContext Does

| Field | Agent side | MCP server side |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| `user_id` | Scopes memory search, conversation history, semantic cache to this user | Not sent (stays on agent) |
| `bearer_token` | Sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on this invocation's tool calls to every HTTP/SSE MCP server (unless its spec sets `forward_caller_token=False`, or has an API key and does not set `forward_caller_token=True`), over a session opened for this token | Validated by `AuthMiddleware`, extracted into `ClientContext` with roles/scopes/claims |
| `roles` | Available for agent-side logic via `get_current_caller()` | Not sent: server extracts roles from the JWT |
| `scopes` | Available for agent-side logic | Not sent: server extracts scopes from the JWT |
| `metadata` | Custom data available to guardrails, hooks, events | Not sent |

### Identity Flow: Agent → MCP Server

```
CallerContext(bearer_token="eyJ...")
    → the tool call goes over an MCP session opened with this token
      (one per caller; never shared with another caller)
        → HTTP request to MCP server with Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
            → AuthMiddleware validates JWT
                → Extracts roles, scopes, claims
                → Builds ClientContext
                    → Guards check HasRole, HasScope
                        → Handler receives ctx.client
```

Only the `bearer_token` crosses the wire. Everything else is extracted server-side from the JWT payload.

### Per-User Isolation

When `CallerContext` is passed, these features automatically isolate per user:

```python
agent = await build_agent(
    ...,
    memory=ChromaProvider(...),          # Memory scoped to caller.user_id
    conversation_store=SQLiteStore(...), # Sessions owned by caller.user_id
    cache=SemanticCache(),               # Cache keyed by caller.user_id
    observe=True,                        # Traces tagged with caller.user_id
)

# Alice and Bob have completely separate state
await agent.chat("question", session_id="s1", caller=alice_ctx)
await agent.chat("question", session_id="s2", caller=bob_ctx)
```

### Accessing CallerContext in Custom Code

```python
from promptise.agent import get_current_caller

# Inside guardrails, hooks, or other code running in an invocation:
caller = get_current_caller()
if caller:
    print(caller.user_id)    # "user-alice-001"
    print(caller.roles)      # {"analyst", "viewer"}
```

A `@tool` function takes the caller as a parameter instead: annotate one
`CallerContext` and the agent fills it in, hidden from the model (see
[Tools → The caller](../tools.md#the-caller)).

See [CallerContext: Agent to MCP Identity](../../guides/multi-user-identity.md) for the complete end-to-end guide with JWT structure, guard reference, and server-side handler examples.

## From Agent to Production: Governance & Runtime

`build_agent()` creates a request-response agent: you call it, it replies. That's perfect for chatbots and synchronous workflows. For **autonomous agents** that run continuously, respond to triggers, and need safety rails, you wrap the agent in an **AgentProcess** managed by the **AgentRuntime**.

The runtime adds three capability layers on top of any agent you build with `build_agent()`:

### Triggers: how the agent wakes up

Instead of calling `ainvoke()` manually, you configure triggers that fire automatically:

- **Cron**: run on a schedule (every 5 minutes, hourly, daily at midnight)
- **Webhook**: listen for HTTP POSTs from monitoring systems, CI/CD pipelines, or APIs
- **File Watch**: react to filesystem changes
- **Event**: subscribe to an in-process EventBus shared with other agents
- **Message**: receive topic-based messages from a MessageBroker

Multiple triggers can fire on the same agent. See [Triggers](../../runtime/triggers/index.md).

### Governance: guardrails against runaway behavior

Four opt-in subsystems, each disabled by default with zero overhead:

| Subsystem | What it prevents | Docs |
|-----------|------------------|------|
| **Autonomy Budget** | Tool-call runaway loops, unexpected costs, unbounded irreversible actions | [Autonomy Budget](../../runtime/governance/budget.md) |
| **Behavioral Health** | Stuck agents, repeating loops, empty responses, elevated error rates | [Behavioral Health](../../runtime/governance/health.md) |
| **Mission Model** | Long-horizon trajectory drift from the agent's objective | [Mission Model](../../runtime/governance/mission.md) |
| **Secret Scoping** | Credential leakage, secrets in logs, keys stored as plaintext in memory | [Secret Scoping](../../runtime/governance/secrets.md) |

```python
from promptise.runtime import (
    AgentRuntime, ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig,
    BudgetConfig, HealthConfig, MissionConfig,
)

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Monitor the data pipeline.",
    servers={"tools": {"type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp"}},
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="webhook", webhook_path="/alerts", webhook_port=9090),
    ],

    # Budget: prevent runaway tool calls
    budget=BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,
        max_tool_calls_per_run=20,
        max_cost_per_day=50.0,
        on_exceeded="pause",
    ),

    # Health: catch stuck agents
    health=HealthConfig(
        enabled=True,
        stuck_threshold=3,
        on_anomaly="escalate",
    ),

    # Mission: evaluate progress every 10 invocations
    mission=MissionConfig(
        enabled=True,
        objective="Keep all services above 99.9% uptime.",
        success_criteria="No unresolved P1 incidents for >15 minutes.",
        eval_every=10,
    ),
)

async with AgentRuntime() as runtime:
    await runtime.add_process("pipeline-observer", config)
    await runtime.start_all()
    # Process runs autonomously until stopped.
```

### Persistence: journal, crash recovery, audit trail

The **FileJournal** records every state transition, trigger event, invocation, and tool call to an append-only JSONL file on disk. On crash, the **ReplayEngine** reconstructs the last known state so the agent can pick up where it left off.

The journal is also your audit trail. Every decision the agent made is timestamped, structured, and greppable.

### When to use the runtime

| If you're building... | Use |
|----------------------|-----|
| A chatbot or Q&A interface | `build_agent()` alone + `chat()` with `conversation_store` |
| A one-shot automation script | `build_agent()` alone + `ainvoke()` |
| A background worker that wakes on a schedule | `AgentProcess` with cron trigger |
| An incident responder that reacts to webhooks | `AgentProcess` with webhook trigger |
| A file processor that reacts to new files | `AgentProcess` with file_watch trigger |
| A multi-agent pipeline | `AgentRuntime` with multiple processes + event triggers |
| Any agent that spends real money autonomously | Always add `BudgetConfig` with `on_exceeded="pause"` |

See the full [Agent Runtime](../../runtime/index.md) docs for architecture, state machine, and deployment patterns.

---

## API Summary

| Symbol | Import | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `build_agent()` | `from promptise import build_agent` | Async factory that discovers tools and returns a `PromptiseAgent`. |
| `tool` | `from promptise import tool` | Decorator that makes a Python function a tool for `extra_tools`. |
| `ToolError` | `from promptise import ToolError` | Raise in a tool to send the model an error it can act on. |
| `PromptiseAgent` | `from promptise.agent import PromptiseAgent` | Unified agent with `ainvoke()`, `astream()`, `invoke()`, `shutdown()`, `get_stats()`, `generate_report()`. |
| `ServerSpec` | `from promptise.config import ServerSpec` | Union type: `StdioServerSpec \| HTTPServerSpec`. |
| `CrossAgent` | `from promptise.cross_agent import CrossAgent` | Peer agent wrapper with `agent` and `description` fields. |
| `CallerContext` | `from promptise.agent import CallerContext` | Per-request identity: user_id, bearer_token, roles, scopes, metadata. |
| `get_current_caller()` | `from promptise.agent import get_current_caller` | Get the CallerContext for the current invocation (from contextvar). |
| `PromptiseSecurityScanner` | `from promptise import PromptiseSecurityScanner` | Composable security scanner for input/output guardrails. |

!!! tip "Model strings"
    Promptise uses LangChain's `init_chat_model()` under the hood, so any provider string it accepts works here: `"openai:gpt-5-mini"`, `"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-20250514"`, `"ollama:llama3"`, etc.

!!! tip "Empty server dict"
    Passing an empty `servers={}` is valid. The agent runs without MCP tools: useful when you only need `extra_tools` or `cross_agents`.

!!! warning "Always await shutdown"
    Forgetting `await agent.shutdown()` can leak open connections to MCP servers. Use a `try/finally` block or wrap the agent lifecycle in an async context manager pattern.

# Tools

An agent calls two kinds of tools: Python functions you declare with `@tool`
and pass to `build_agent(extra_tools=[...])`, and the tools of the MCP servers
it connects to.  This page covers both: first how to declare a tool, then how
MCP tools are discovered and their JSON Schemas converted.

**Source:** `src/promptise/function_tools.py` (`@tool`), `src/promptise/tools.py` (MCP tools)

## Declare tools with `@tool`

Decorate a function with `@tool` and give it to the agent:

```python
import asyncio
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import Field

from promptise import CallerContext, ToolError, build_agent, tool

ORDERS = {"A-1001": {"order_id": "A-1001", "status": "shipped", "total": 120.0}}


@tool
async def get_order(order_id: str, include_lines: bool = False) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, for example "A-1001".
        include_lines: Also return the order lines.
    """
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise ToolError(f"No order {order_id}. Check the ID with the customer.")
    return order


@tool(name="refund_order", timeout=10)
def refund(
    order_id: str,
    amount: Annotated[float, Field(gt=0, description="Amount to refund, in EUR.")],
    caller: CallerContext,
) -> str:
    """Refund part of an order."""
    return f"Refunded {amount:.2f} EUR on {order_id} for {caller.user_id}."


async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", extra_tools=[get_order, refund])
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Refund 20 EUR on order A-1001."}]},
        caller=CallerContext(user_id="alice"),
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()


asyncio.run(main())
```

`@tool` works bare, with options (`@tool(name=..., description=..., timeout=...)`)
and with the name alone (`@tool("get_order")`), on `async def` and plain `def`
functions.  `extra_tools` also takes a plain function as it is (it is made a
tool as if decorated) and LangChain tools.

### What the model sees

The tool's **name** is the function's name.  Its **description** is the
docstring without the parameter section; the parameter section describes the
parameters instead.  The **parameters** come from the type hints, defaults
and `Field` constraints.  For `get_order` the model is offered:

```json
{
  "name": "get_order",
  "description": "Look up an order by its ID.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "The order ID, for example \"A-1001\"."},
      "include_lines": {"type": "boolean", "default": false, "description": "Also return the order lines."}
    },
    "required": ["order_id"]
  }
}
```

`refund_order` takes `order_id` (a string) and `amount`, both required:

```json
{"type": "number", "exclusiveMinimum": 0, "description": "Amount to refund, in EUR."}
```

`caller` is not in the schema: the agent fills it in (see
[The caller](#the-caller)).  A function decorated with `@server.tool()` on a
Promptise MCP server gets the same parameter schema, built by the same code,
so a tool keeps its parameters when it moves between your agent and an MCP
server.  (An MCP server describes the tool with the docstring's first
paragraph only.)

### Describing parameters

A parameter's description comes from the first of these that is present:

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| `Field(description=...)` in `Annotated` or as the default | `amount: Annotated[float, Field(gt=0, description="Amount to refund.")]` |
| A string in `Annotated` | `reason: Annotated[str, "Why the customer wants a refund."]` |
| The docstring, Google style | `Args:` then `order_id: The order ID.` |
| The docstring, NumPy style | `Parameters` / `----------` then `order_id : str` and an indented description |
| The docstring, Sphinx style | `:param order_id: The order ID.` |

Pass `description=` to `@tool` to send the model a different tool
description.  A function without a docstring is described by its name, so
write one: the model decides when to call a tool from its description.

### Types and validation

Every type Pydantic understands works: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`,
`Optional[...]` / `X | None`, `Literal[...]`, `Enum`, `list[...]`,
`dict[str, ...]`, `datetime` / `date`, nested Pydantic models (inlined into
the schema, without `$ref`), and constraints such as `Field(ge=1, le=100)`,
`max_length` or `pattern`.  A parameter without a type hint is a string.

The arguments are validated before the function runs.  The function gets
them in its own types (a nested model as an instance, an enum as its member,
defaults filled in), and lax conversions apply (`"12.5"` for a `float`).  An
explicit `null` for an optional parameter that can't be `None` counts as not
given, and a nested object the model sent as JSON text is decoded.  When the
arguments don't fit, the function does not run and the model gets a tool
error it can correct:

```text
Invalid arguments for tool 'refund_order':
- amount: Input should be greater than 0 (got -20)
Correct the arguments and call the tool again.
```

Arguments that are not JSON at all (a Python-style dict with single quotes, a
cut-off object) never reach the function.  The agent answers the call with an
error that says what is wrong and names the tool's parameters, and the model
can call again:

```text
Error: The arguments for 'refund_order' were not valid JSON (Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes at line 1 column 2). Call the tool again with a JSON object that matches its parameters: order_id (required), amount (required).
```

### The caller

A parameter annotated `CallerContext` receives the caller of the current
`agent.ainvoke(..., caller=...)` or `agent.chat(..., caller=...)`: the user's
id, tenant, roles, scopes and metadata, to scope a query or check a
permission.  It is never part of the schema, so the model can't set it.
Without a caller the parameter gets an empty `CallerContext()` (no user, no
roles); annotate it `CallerContext | None` to get `None` instead.  It works
in sync and async tools, and in a peer agent the caller is the one the first
agent was invoked with.

```python
@tool
async def my_orders(status: str, caller: CallerContext) -> list:
    """List the caller's orders with a status."""
    if "support" not in caller.roles:
        raise ToolError("Only support staff can list orders.")
    return await db.orders.list(owner=caller.user_id, status=status)
```

### Errors

Raise `ToolError` (from `promptise`, the same class MCP server tools raise) to
give the model an error it can act on.  The model gets the error envelope a
Promptise MCP server sends, and the call counts as failed in events,
observability and streaming:

```json
{"error": {"code": "TOOL_ERROR", "message": "No order A-9999. Check the ID with the customer.", "retryable": false}}
```

`ToolError` takes `code=`, `retryable=` and `suggestion=` as well, and the
other `MCPError` subclasses (`RateLimitError`, `ValidationError` ...) are
reported the same way.  Any other exception is a tool that failed, as for
every tool: the model reads `Error: <type>: <message>`, so don't put secrets
in exception messages.

With `timeout=` a call that runs longer is answered with a `TIMEOUT` error
(`Tool 'refund_order' did not finish within 10s, so its outcome is unknown.`).
An async function is cancelled; a sync function's thread can't be stopped, so
it finishes in the background and its result is dropped (the error says it is
still running). The call may have taken effect before it was stopped, so the
error is `retryable` only for a tool marked `@tool(read_only=True)` or
`@tool(idempotent=True)`; for any other tool it tells the model to check
whether the call took effect before calling it again. `read_only` and
`idempotent` are the MCP `readOnlyHint` and `idempotentHint` annotations, so
the semantic cache and approval rules read them too.

### Results

| The function returns | The model reads |
|---|---|
| `str` | The string as it is |
| `None` | An empty result |
| `dict`, `list`, `tuple`, numbers, `bool` | JSON (`{"status": "shipped"}`, `["a", "b"]`, `42`, `true`) |
| A Pydantic model or dataclass | Its fields as JSON |
| `datetime`, `Enum`, `set` inside the value | ISO strings, the enum's value, a list |

Non-ASCII text stays readable (`"Zürich"`, not `"Z\u00fcrich"`).  With
`agent_pattern="code-action"` the program gets the value back as data (a
dict, a list), not as JSON text.

### Sync and async functions

An `async def` tool runs on the event loop.  A plain `def` tool runs in a
worker thread, so a blocking call (a database driver, `requests`) never
stalls the agent or other tool calls running in parallel.

### Testing a tool

A tool stays callable like the function it was made from, so unit tests call
it directly, without validation or an agent:

```python
assert (await get_order("A-1001"))["status"] == "shipped"
assert refund("A-1001", 20.0, CallerContext(user_id="alice")).startswith("Refunded")
```

`await get_order.ainvoke({"order_id": "A-1001"})` runs it the way the agent
does (validated, with the caller injected) and returns the text the model
reads.

To test the agent that calls your tools without a model provider, script the
model's tool calls with `ScriptedModel` (see [Testing Agents](testing.md)).

### Approval, guardrails and tracing

A `@tool` is a LangChain `BaseTool`, so everything that applies to tools
applies to it, by its name: `ApprovalPolicy(tools=["refund_*"])` gates it
(invalid arguments are rejected before a reviewer is asked), guardrails with
`scan_tool_results=True` scan its result before the model reads it, and
`trace_tools`, `observe`, `events` and `optimize_tools` include it.

!!! note "LangChain tools still work"
    `extra_tools` accepts LangChain tools as well (`@tool` from
    `langchain_core.tools`, `StructuredTool`, any `BaseTool`), so existing
    code keeps working.  Switching a simple tool to `from promptise import
    tool` changes nothing the model sees: the name, description and
    parameter schema are the same.  For a docstring with an `Args:` section
    the parameter descriptions move from the tool description into the
    parameters, as with LangChain's `parse_docstring=True`.

## MCP tools

The `tools` module discovers MCP tools and converts them into fully-typed
LangChain `BaseTool` instances.  Its centrepiece is the recursive JSON Schema
to Pydantic converter that ensures LLMs see rich, described parameter types
-- including nested objects, arrays, unions, enums, and `$ref`/`$defs` -- so
they can generate correct tool calls on the first attempt.

### Discovering MCP tools

```python
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent, StdioServerSpec

async def main():
    # build_agent discovers and converts tools internally
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={
            "math": StdioServerSpec(command="python", args=["-m", "math_server"]),
        },
    )
    # Agent has discovered all tools from connected MCP servers
    for tool in agent.tools:
        print(f"{tool.name}: {tool.description}")

    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 123 * 456?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

asyncio.run(main())
```

### Concepts

#### ToolInfo

A frozen dataclass that holds human-friendly metadata about a discovered MCP
tool.  Useful for introspection, debugging, and building tool registries.

```python
from promptise.tools import ToolInfo

info = ToolInfo(
    server_guess="math",
    name="add",
    description="Add two numbers",
    input_schema={
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "a": {"type": "number", "description": "First operand"},
            "b": {"type": "number", "description": "Second operand"},
        },
        "required": ["a", "b"],
    },
)
print(info.name)          # "add"
print(info.description)   # "Add two numbers"
```

#### MCPClientError

Raised when communication with the MCP client fails -- for example, when
listing tools or calling a tool over a broken connection.

```python
from promptise.tools import MCPClientError

try:
    # ... attempt to call an MCP tool ...
    pass
except MCPClientError as exc:
    print(f"MCP communication failed: {exc}")
```

#### JSON Schema to Pydantic conversion

The core of the module is the `_jsonschema_to_pydantic` function (internal) that
recursively converts a JSON Schema dict into a Pydantic model.  This is critical
for tool-calling accuracy: without proper nested models, the LLM only sees `dict`
and has to guess the structure.

The converter handles:

| JSON Schema feature | Python/Pydantic result |
|---------------------|----------------------|
| `"type": "string"` | `str` |
| `"type": "integer"` | `int` |
| `"type": "number"` | `float` |
| `"type": "boolean"` | `bool` |
| `"type": "array"` | `list` or `list[T]` with typed items |
| `"type": "object"` with `properties` | Nested Pydantic `BaseModel` |
| `"enum": [...]` | `Literal["a", "b", "c"]` |
| `"anyOf"` / `"oneOf"` | `Union[...]` or `Optional[...]` |
| `"allOf"` | Merged properties |
| `"$ref"` / `"$defs"` | Resolved and inlined |
| `"default"` | Pydantic `Field(default=...)` |
| `"description"` | Pydantic `Field(description=...)` |

Example of a complex schema being converted:

```python
# MCP tool exposes this JSON Schema:
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "query": {"type": "string", "description": "Search query"},
        "filters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "date_from": {"type": "string", "description": "ISO date"},
                "limit": {"type": "integer", "default": 10},
            },
        },
        "tags": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {"type": "string"},
        },
    },
    "required": ["query"],
}

# Promptise converts this to a Pydantic model equivalent to:
# class Filters(BaseModel):
#     date_from: str | None = Field(None, description="ISO date")
#     limit: int = Field(10)
#
# class SearchArgs(BaseModel):
#     query: str = Field(..., description="Search query")
#     filters: Filters | None = None
#     tags: list[str] | None = None
```

#### MCPToolAdapter

For direct tool discovery and conversion outside of `build_agent`, use
`MCPToolAdapter` from the Promptise MCP Client.  It connects to MCP servers
via `MCPMultiClient`, discovers all available tools, converts their schemas
to Pydantic models, and wraps each tool in a LangChain `BaseTool`.

```python
import asyncio
from promptise import MCPClient, MCPMultiClient, MCPToolAdapter

async def main():
    multi = MCPMultiClient({
        "math": MCPClient(url="http://localhost:8080/mcp"),
    })

    async with multi:
        adapter = MCPToolAdapter(multi)
        tools = await adapter.as_langchain_tools()

        for tool in tools:
            print(f"Tool: {tool.name} -- {tool.description}")

        # For debugging: get tool metadata without creating BaseTool wrappers
        infos = await adapter.list_tool_info()
        for info in infos:
            print(f"{info.server_guess}/{info.name}: {info.input_schema}")

asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Callback hooks

`MCPToolAdapter` supports three callback hooks for tracing tool calls:

```python
def on_before(tool_name: str, arguments: dict) -> None:
    """Called before each tool invocation."""
    print(f"Calling {tool_name} with {arguments}")

def on_after(tool_name: str, result: Any) -> None:
    """Called after each tool invocation."""
    print(f"{tool_name} returned: {result}")

def on_error(tool_name: str, error: Exception) -> None:
    """Called when a tool invocation fails."""
    print(f"{tool_name} failed: {error}")

adapter = MCPToolAdapter(
    multi,
    on_before=on_before,
    on_after=on_after,
    on_error=on_error,
)
```

### API summary

#### ToolInfo

| Attribute | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `server_guess` | `str` | Best-guess server name the tool belongs to |
| `name` | `str` | Tool name |
| `description` | `str` | Human-readable tool description |
| `input_schema` | `dict[str, Any]` | Raw JSON Schema for the tool's input |

#### MCPClientError

| Base class | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| `RuntimeError` | Raised when MCP client communication fails |

#### MCPToolAdapter

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `multi` | `MCPMultiClient` | *required* | Connected multi-server client |
| `on_before` | `OnBefore \| None` | `None` | Callback before each tool call |
| `on_after` | `OnAfter \| None` | `None` | Callback after each tool call |
| `on_error` | `OnError \| None` | `None` | Callback on tool errors |

| Method | Returns | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `as_langchain_tools()` | `list[BaseTool]` | Discover all tools and return as LangChain tools |
| `list_tool_info()` | `list[ToolInfo]` | Return tool metadata for introspection |

#### Callback types

| Type | Signature |
|------|-----------|
| `OnBefore` | `Callable[[str, dict[str, Any]], None]` |
| `OnAfter` | `Callable[[str, Any], None]` |
| `OnError` | `Callable[[str, Exception], None]` |

### Tips and gotchas

!!! tip
    You rarely need to use `MCPToolAdapter` directly.  `build_agent` handles
    tool discovery internally.  The returned `PromptiseAgent` contains all
    discovered tools.

!!! warning
    If an MCP server is unreachable during tool discovery, `MCPToolAdapter`
    raises `MCPClientError` with diagnostic information.  Check server URLs,
    network connectivity, and authentication headers.

!!! tip
    Use `list_tool_info()` for debugging tool discovery without creating
    actual `BaseTool` wrappers.  It returns lightweight `ToolInfo` dataclass
    instances.

!!! warning
    Tool name collisions across servers are possible.  If two servers expose
    a tool with the same name, the server listed last in `servers` wins:
    the agent gets only that server's copy, and a warning is logged.  Use
    server-specific tool name prefixes on your MCP servers to avoid this.

# Testing Agents

An agent's behavior depends on what the model answers, and a real model costs
money, needs an API key and answers differently from run to run.
`promptise.testing.ScriptedModel` takes the model's place: you write its
replies in advance, the agent runs exactly as it would with a provider (tools
are bound and called, results go back to the model, streaming works), and the
model records every request it received so you can assert on it.

Nothing leaves the process, so these tests run in CI without secrets, and
you don't import LangChain to write them.

**Source:** `src/promptise/testing.py`

## A first test

Script one tool call and the final answer, run the agent, and check both the
answer and what the model was sent:

```python
import asyncio
import json

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall

ORDERS = {"A-1001": {"order_id": "A-1001", "status": "shipped"}}


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, for example "A-1001".
    """
    return ORDERS[order_id]


async def ask(model: ScriptedModel, question: str) -> str:
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    try:
        result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
    finally:
        await agent.shutdown()
    return result["messages"][-1].content


def test_agent_looks_up_the_order():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])

    answer = asyncio.run(ask(model, "Where is order A-1001?"))

    assert answer == "Order A-1001 has shipped."
    # The model was called twice, with the get_order tool bound both times.
    assert [call.tools for call in model.calls] == [["get_order"], ["get_order"]]
    # The second call carried the tool's result.
    assert model.calls[1].messages[-1].content == json.dumps(ORDERS["A-1001"])
```

Run it with `pytest`.  The test wraps the agent in `asyncio.run()`, so it
needs no plugin; with `pytest-asyncio` you can write `async def` tests and
`await` the agent directly.

Each model call takes the next reply.  The first reply asks for `get_order`,
the agent runs the real tool, and the second reply is the answer.  The tool
itself is not mocked: only the model is scripted.

## Replies

A reply is one model turn.  It can be:

| Reply | The model's turn |
|---|---|
| `"text"` | Text with no tool calls: the agent's answer |
| `ToolCall(name, args)` | One tool call |
| `[ToolCall(...), ToolCall(...)]` | Several tool calls in one turn (the agent runs them in parallel); a string in the list is the turn's text |
| `Malformed.tool_call_as_text(...)` | A tool call written into the text instead of sent as one |
| `Malformed.unparseable_arguments(...)` | A tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON |
| an `AIMessage` | That LangChain message, as it is |

`ToolCall(name, args, id=None)` takes the tool's name and arguments.  Leave
`id` out and the model numbers its calls `call_1`, `call_2`, ... in the order
it sends them, so the ids in a test are always the same.

A reply that isn't one of these raises `TypeError` when the model is created,
so a typo in a script fails at once rather than in the middle of a run.

## Assert on what the model received

`model.calls` holds a `ModelCall` for every request, in order:

| Attribute | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `messages` | The messages the model was sent (system prompt, conversation, tool results) |
| `tools` | The names of the tools bound for that call |
| `tool_schemas` | Those tools as the model was offered them (OpenAI-style function definitions) |
| `reply` | The message the model answered with (`None` when it had no reply left) |

`model.remaining` is the number of replies not yet sent.  Checking it at the
end of a test shows that the agent made as many model calls as you expected:

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}), "Shipped."])
    agent = await build_agent(
        model=model,
        instructions="You answer questions about orders.",
        extra_tools=[get_order],
    )
    await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    first = model.calls[0]
    print(first.messages[0].type, "|", first.messages[0].content[:33])
    print(first.messages[-1].type, "|", first.messages[-1].content)
    print(first.tool_schemas[0]["function"]["parameters"]["required"])
    print(model.calls[1].messages[-1].type, model.calls[1].messages[-1].tool_call_id)
    print("replies left:", model.remaining)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
system | You answer questions about orders
human | Where is A-1001?
['order_id']
tool call_1
replies left: 0
```

The messages are LangChain message objects: `.type` is `"system"`, `"human"`,
`"ai"` or `"tool"`, and `.content` is the text.  A tool result also has
`.tool_call_id` and `.status` (`"success"` or `"error"`).

## Test failure handling

Small and local models get tool calling wrong more often than large hosted
ones: they invent tool names, send arguments that don't match the schema or
aren't JSON, or write the tool call into their text.  Scripting these replies tests what your
agent does when it happens, without waiting for a model to make the mistake.

### A tool name the agent doesn't have

Script a `ToolCall` with a name the agent has no tool for.  The agent doesn't
fail: the model gets an error result that names the tools it can call, and its
next turn can use the right one.

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


@tool
def refund_order(order_id: str, amount: float) -> str:
    """Refund part of an order."""
    return f"Refunded {amount:.2f} EUR on {order_id}."


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order_status", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),  # invented name
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),         # the model corrects it
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order, refund_order])
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    error = model.calls[1].messages[-1]
    print(error.status, "|", error.content)
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
error | Error: Unknown tool 'get_order_status'. Call one of the available tools: get_order, refund_order.
Order A-1001 has shipped.
```

The error lists the agent's tools with the names closest to the one called
first, at most 20 of them, followed by how many more there are.  When the
name looks like a misspelling of a tool's name (`get_ordr`, `getOrder`), the
error also asks "Did you mean 'get_order'?".  A name that only shares a word
with a tool, such as `cancel_order`, gets no suggestion, so the model isn't
pointed at a tool that does something else.

### Invalid arguments

Arguments that don't match the tool's schema are a `ToolCall` too.  A
[`@tool`](tools.md) function checks its arguments before it runs, and the
model gets the problems to correct:

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order", {"id": "A-1001"}),        # wrong argument name
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    print(model.calls[1].messages[-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
Invalid arguments for tool 'get_order':
- order_id: Field required
Correct the arguments and call the tool again.
```

### A tool call written as text

Some models answer with the tool call as JSON in their text instead of as a
tool call.  `Malformed.tool_call_as_text(name, args)` sends that reply, in one
of three styles:

| `style` | Text of the reply |
|---|---|
| `"json"` (default) | `{"name": "get_order", "arguments": {"order_id": "A-1001"}}` |
| `"tagged"` | The same object inside `<tool_call>` and `</tool_call>` lines |
| `"fenced"` | The same object in a Markdown `json` code block |

The reply has no tool call, so the agent takes the text as the answer and no
tool runs.  A test can check that your code catches such an answer, for
example a check that rejects answers that look like JSON:

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import Malformed, ScriptedModel


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


def looks_like_a_tool_call(answer: str) -> bool:
    text = answer.strip().strip("`").removeprefix("json").strip()
    return text.startswith(("{", "<tool_call>")) and '"name"' in text


async def main():
    for style in ("json", "tagged", "fenced"):
        model = ScriptedModel([
            Malformed.tool_call_as_text("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}, style=style),
        ])
        agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
        result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
        await agent.shutdown()
        answer = result["messages"][-1].content
        print(style, looks_like_a_tool_call(answer))


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
json True
tagged True
fenced True
```

### Arguments that aren't JSON

`Malformed.unparseable_arguments(name, raw_args)` sends a tool call whose
argument text can't be parsed, such as a Python-style dict with single
quotes (the default).  LangChain keeps such a call in the message's
`invalid_tool_calls`, not its `tool_calls`, as it does for a provider's reply.
The agent doesn't run a call it can't read.  It answers the call with a tool
error (`status="error"`, the call's own `tool_call_id`) that says what is
wrong and names the tool's parameters, and the loop goes on, so the model can
call the tool again:

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import Malformed, ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        Malformed.unparseable_arguments("get_order", "{'order_id': 'A-1001'}"),
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),  # the model calls again
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    error = model.calls[1].messages[-1]
    print(error.status, error.tool_call_id)
    print(error.content)
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
error call_1
Error: The arguments for 'get_order' were not valid JSON (Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes at line 1 column 2). Call the tool again with a JSON object that matches its parameters: order_id (required).
Order A-1001 has shipped.
```

Such a call counts as a failed tool call: `NodeResult.tool_calls` records it
with `success: False`, `invalid: True` and the text the model sent under
`raw_args`, callbacks get its start and an `on_tool_error`
(`ToolArgumentError`), and `astream_with_tools()` yields a `ToolEndEvent`
with `success=False`.  Each retry is a model call, so `max_agent_iterations`
still ends a model that never sends valid arguments.  A call that names a tool
the agent doesn't have gets the
[unknown-tool error](#a-tool-name-the-agent-doesnt-have) instead.

When this reply is streamed, LangChain reads the arguments as a partial JSON
object, as it does for a provider's stream: a cut-off object such as
`'{"order_id"'` becomes a tool call with the arguments read so far (`{}`),
while text that can't start a JSON object stays an invalid call and gets the
same error.  A streamed run (`astream_with_tools()`) recovers the same way.

## When the replies run out

A model call after the last reply raises `ScriptExhaustedError`, which says
which call it was and how many replies the script has.  In an agent run it
fails the run: `ainvoke()` raises `GraphExecutionError`, whose `__cause__` is
the `ScriptExhaustedError`.  An agent that makes more model calls than you
scripted is usually the bug a test is looking for, so this is the default.

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.engine import GraphExecutionError
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ScriptExhaustedError


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel(["Hello!"])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model)
    ask = {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}]}
    await agent.ainvoke(ask)
    try:
        await agent.ainvoke(ask)
    except GraphExecutionError as exc:
        assert isinstance(exc.__cause__, ScriptExhaustedError)
        print(exc.__cause__)
    finally:
        await agent.shutdown()


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
ScriptedModel has no reply for model call 2: the script has 1 reply. Add a reply, or pass on_exhausted='repeat_last' to repeat the last one.
```

The call is still recorded in `model.calls`, with `reply=None`, so you can
see what the agent asked for.

`ScriptedModel(replies, on_exhausted="repeat_last")` answers every call after
the last reply with the last reply again, for a test that calls the agent
many times with the same answer.  A script with no replies raises either way.

## Streaming and sync calls

The model streams too.  Its text comes word by word and each tool call as one
chunk, so `astream_with_tools()` and `astream()` emit the same events as with
a provider:

```python
import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    async for event in agent.astream_with_tools(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]}
    ):
        if event.type == "token":
            print(f"token {event.text!r}")
        else:
            print(event.type)
    await agent.shutdown()


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
tool_start
tool_end
token 'Order '
token 'A-1001 '
token 'has '
token 'shipped.'
done
```

`model.invoke()` and `model.stream()` work as well, for code that calls a
chat model synchronously:

```python
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel

model = ScriptedModel(["Bonjour", "Hello there"])
print(model.invoke("Say hello in French").content)
print([chunk.content for chunk in model.stream("Now in English") if chunk.content])
```

Output:

```
Bonjour
['Hello ', 'there']
```

## Where to use it

`ScriptedModel` is a LangChain chat model, so it goes wherever a model
instance is accepted: `build_agent(model=...)`, every agent pattern
(`agent_pattern="react"`, `"peoatr"`, your own `PromptGraph`), a
[`FallbackChain`](fallback.md) and a graph node's model.  Tools are bound
with `bind_tools()` as for a provider model, and `calls` records the tools of
each call.

Things to know:

- **The replies don't depend on the input.**  A script fixes the order of
  the model's turns, not what it reads.  Assert on `model.calls` to check
  what the agent sent; to make a reply depend on the conversation, script an
  `AIMessage` you build in the test, or subclass the model.
- **There is no token usage.**  Replies carry no usage data, so budgets and
  cost reports see zero tokens.
- **An `AgentProcess` runs on it too.**  Pass it as the process's model,
  `ProcessConfig(model=ScriptedModel([...]))` or
  `AgentProcess(name, config, model=...)`, and inject a `TriggerEvent`: the
  process runs the agent on the script without a provider
  ([The agent's model](../runtime/processes.md#the-agents-model)).
- **Concurrent runs share the script.**  Each call takes the next reply
  whichever run makes it, so give each concurrent run its own model.

## API summary

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ScriptedModel(replies, *, on_exhausted="raise")` | The chat model; `calls`, `remaining` |
| `ToolCall(name, args={}, id=None)` | A tool call in a reply |
| `Malformed.tool_call_as_text(name, args=None, *, style="json")` | A tool call written as text |
| `Malformed.unparseable_arguments(name, raw_args="{'arg': 'value'}", *, id=None)` | A tool call whose arguments are not JSON |
| `ModelCall` | One recorded request: `messages`, `tools`, `tool_schemas`, `reply` |
| `ScriptExhaustedError` | Raised by a call after the last reply (a `RuntimeError`) |

All of them are imported from `promptise.testing`.

- [Streaming](streaming.md) -- the events `astream_with_tools()` emits
- [Custom Reasoning Patterns](agents/reasoning-patterns.md) -- graphs you can test the same way
