# Graph Edges & Transitions

Edges define how the graph flows from one node to another. The engine resolves transitions dynamically at runtime using a 7-step priority system.

## Edge Dataclass

```python
from promptise.engine import Edge, NodeResult


def my_fn(result: NodeResult) -> bool:
    return result.error is None


Edge(
    from_node="plan",       # Source node name
    to_node="act",          # Target node name
    condition=my_fn,        # Optional: (NodeResult) -> bool
    label="ready",          # Optional: label for visualization
    priority=0,             # Optional: higher = checked first
)
```

## Edge Helpers

All helpers return `self` for chaining: `graph.always("a", "b").always("b", "c")`.

### always: Unconditional

```python
graph.always("plan", "execute")   # plan always goes to execute
```

### when: Conditional

```python
graph.when("review", "fix",
    condition=lambda result: (result.output if isinstance(result.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) < 3,
    label="low_quality",
)
```

### on_tool_call / on_no_tool_call: Tool-based routing

```python
graph.on_tool_call("gather", "summarize")   # After a node that made tool calls
graph.on_no_tool_call("gather", "__end__")  # After a node that made none
```

A `PromptNode` whose model called tools is re-entered by the engine before any
edge is checked (step 1 below), so these edges matter for nodes that record
tool calls without asking for that re-entry: a `ToolNode`, a `ParallelNode`, a
`FanOutNode`, a custom node. After a `PromptNode`, `on_no_tool_call` is the
edge that applies once the model answers without tools.

### on_output: Output key matching

```python
graph.on_output("review", "publish", key="approved", value=True)
graph.on_output("review", "revise", key="approved", value=False)
```

### on_error: Error routing

```python
graph.on_error("risky_step", "fallback")   # Route to fallback if node errors
```

### on_confidence: Confidence threshold

```python
graph.on_confidence("analyze", "conclude", min_confidence=0.7)
# Routes to "conclude" when output["confidence"] >= 0.7
```

### on_guard_fail: Guard failure routing

```python
graph.on_guard_fail("validate", "revise")
# Routes to "revise" when any guard fails
```

### sequential: Chain multiple nodes

```python
graph.sequential("step1", "step2", "step3", "step4")
# Creates: step1 → step2 → step3 → step4 (always edges)
```

### loop_until: Conditional loop with exit

```python
graph.loop_until("refine", "deliver",
    condition=lambda result: (result.output if isinstance(result.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) >= 4,
    max_iterations=5,
)
# Loops "refine" until quality >= 4, then exits to "deliver"
# Exit edge gets priority=10, loop edge gets priority=0
```

`refine` runs at most `max_iterations` times in a run (fewer if its own `max_iterations` is lower). Once it has used them, the engine exits to `deliver` even though the condition never held. `max_iterations` below 1 raises `ValueError`.

### Low-level add_edge

```python
graph.add_edge("a", "b", condition=my_fn, label="custom", priority=10)
```

### Helper reference

| Helper | Condition | Label |
|--------|-----------|-------|
| `always(a, b)` | none | `""` |
| `when(a, b, condition, label="")` | your `(NodeResult) -> bool` | `label` |
| `on_tool_call(a, b)` | `result.tool_calls` is not empty | `tool_called` |
| `on_no_tool_call(a, b)` | `result.tool_calls` is empty | `no_tools` |
| `on_output(a, b, key, value=True)` | `result.output` is a dict and `output[key] == value` | `key=value` |
| `on_error(a, b)` | `result.error` is set | `error` |
| `on_confidence(a, b, min_confidence=0.7)` | `result.output` is a dict and `float(output.get("confidence", 0)) >= min_confidence` | `confidence>=0.7` |
| `on_guard_fail(a, b)` | `result.guards_failed` is not empty | `guard_failed` |
| `sequential(*names)` | `always` between each pair | |
| `loop_until(node, exit_to, *, condition, max_iterations=5)` | exit edge (priority 10) + self edge (priority 0) + budget | `exit_loop` / `loop` |

All helpers have priority 0 except the `loop_until` exit edge. The built-in
conditions are `EdgeCondition` objects (`EdgeCondition(kind, key="", value=True,
min_confidence=0.0)` with `kind` one of `tool_called`, `no_tool_call`,
`output`, `error`, `confidence`, `guard_failed`), so their edges can be
[saved to YAML](engine-serialization.md); a lambda condition cannot.

`result.error` includes notes hooks write on a successful node (a
`TimingHook` budget overrun, a `BudgetHook` stop), so `on_error` fires on
those too. `result.output` is the reply text for a plain-text reply (`None`
on a step that only called tools), so `on_output` and `on_confidence` need a
dict: a node with an `output_schema`, a reasoning node's JSON fields, or a
postprocessor that returns a dict.

A condition that raises is treated as not matching (logged at DEBUG), so
`lambda r: r.output.get("quality") >= 4` silently never fires on a text or
`None` output. Write `(r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get(...)`.
Adding a second conditional edge with the same source, target and priority
logs a warning, since the first one that matches wins.

!!! note "Performance"
    The engine maintains a precomputed adjacency index for **O(1) edge lookup** per transition (instead of scanning all edges). The index is rebuilt lazily when edges are added or removed.

## Transition Resolution

When a node finishes, the engine resolves the next node in this order:

```mermaid
graph TD
    NE[Node Executed] --> TC{Tool calls?}
    TC -->|yes| SAME[Re-enter same node]
    TC -->|no| NR{NodeResult<br/>.next_node?}
    NR -->|yes| TARGET2[Go to next_node]
    NR -->|no| LLM{output.route<br/>set?}
    LLM -->|yes| TARGET[Follow that transition<br/>or go to that node]
    LLM -->|no| EDGE{Conditional<br/>edges?}
    EDGE -->|match| TARGET3[Follow edge]
    EDGE -->|no match| TR{Node transitions<br/>match output?}
    TR -->|yes| TARGET4[Follow transition]
    TR -->|no| DEF{default_next?}
    DEF -->|yes| TARGET5[Go to default]
    DEF -->|no| END[__end__]

    style NE fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style SAME fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

1. **Tool loop**: If tools were called, re-enter the same node so the LLM sees tool results
2. **NodeResult.next_node**: If the node explicitly set the next node in its execute() method (`ValidateNode`'s pass/fail, `PlanNode`'s re-plan)
3. **LLM routing**: If output contains `route`, `_next`, `next_step`, or `goto` naming one of the node's transition keys (follows that transition) or a node in the graph
4. **Graph edges**: Conditional edges checked in priority order (highest first)
5. **Node transitions**: For a dict output, the first `transitions` key whose value in the output is `True`, equals the key, or is any non-empty string
6. **default_next**: Fallback node from the node's configuration
7. **__end__**: Graph terminates

## Edge Priority

When multiple conditional edges exist from the same node, they are checked in **priority order** (highest first). Use this to ensure exit conditions are checked before loop conditions:

```python
# Exit condition checked first (priority 10)
graph.add_edge("refine", "deliver",
    condition=lambda r: (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get("done"),
    label="done", priority=10)

# Loop condition checked second (priority 0)
graph.always("refine", "refine")  # default priority=0
```

## Dynamic LLM Routing

The LLM can choose the next node by including a routing field in its output. Routing reads a structured output, so give the node an `output_schema` (a Pydantic model or a `TypedDict`) with a `route` field:

```python
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Decision(BaseModel):
    route: Literal["search", "answer"]
    reason: str


graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "decide",
    output_schema=Decision,
    transitions={"search": "web_search", "answer": "write"},
))
# The LLM outputs {"route": "search", "reason": "Need more data"}
# → the engine follows the "search" transition to "web_search"

# Supported field names: route, _next, next_step, goto
```

A route value that is a transition key follows that transition; otherwise it must name a node in the graph (or `__end__`). When a node without tools has two or more transitions, the engine lists them in the prompt. The `"error"` transition is reserved: the engine follows it when the node has used its `max_iterations`, and never offers it to the model.

## Runtime Graph Mutation

With `PromptGraphEngine(allow_self_modification=True)` (the default, and what
`build_agent` uses), a node's structured output can carry a `_graph_action`
that changes the run's copy of the graph. The original graph is never
modified, and the engine applies at most `max_mutations_per_run` (default 10)
mutations per run, counting these and the `GraphMutation`s nodes return.

| Action | Output fields | What it does |
|--------|---------------|--------------|
| `add_node` | `_graph_action: "add_node"`, `_node_config: {...}` | Adds a `PromptNode` built with `PromptNode.from_config(_node_config)`. Nothing routes to it unless an edge, transition or route names it |
| `add_edge` | `_graph_action: "add_edge"`, `_from: "a"`, `_to: "b"` | Adds an unconditional edge |
| `skip_to` | `_graph_action: "skip_to"`, `_target: "node_name"` | The target node (or `"__end__"`, a normal finish) runs next, ahead of edges and transitions. An unknown target is logged and ignored |
| `retry_with` | `_graph_action: "retry_with"`, `_context_update: {...}` | Merges `_context_update` into `state.context` and runs the node again; each retry uses the node's `max_iterations` budget |

`add_node` and `add_edge`, like a node's `GraphMutation`s, are offered to the
[`on_graph_mutation` hooks](engine-hooks.md#hook-protocol) first; a blocked
one does not count. Before 1.7.0, `skip_to` to a node was overridden by the
normal transition and `retry_with` did not run the node again.

The model only produces these fields when its `output_schema` has them (or a
reasoning node's JSON reply carries them), so a graph whose schemas don't
declare `_graph_action` is not affected. To rule it
out, create the engine with `allow_self_modification=False`; `build_agent` has
no switch for it.

A node can also return `GraphMutation`s in `NodeResult.graph_mutations`
(`add_node`, `remove_node`, `add_edge`, `remove_edge`); see
[GraphMutation](engine.md#noderesult-nodeevent-graphmutation-executionreport).

================================================================================
Page: Reasoning Graph Node Flags Reference
URL: https://docs.promptise.com/core/engine-flags/
================================================================================

# Node Flags

Every node in a Reasoning Graph declares its capabilities and behaviors through **typed flags**. Flags are checked by the engine at runtime to control execution flow, caching, error handling, and observability.

## Using Flags

```python
from promptise.engine import GraphState, NodeFlag, NodeResult, PromptNode, node

# Set flags on any node
PromptNode("analyze",
    instructions="Analyze the data.",
    flags={NodeFlag.CRITICAL, NodeFlag.OBSERVABLE},
)

# Functional nodes support flags too
@node("validate", flags={NodeFlag.RETRYABLE})
async def validate(state: GraphState) -> NodeResult:
    return NodeResult(output={"ok": True})

# Check flags at runtime (@node returns a node object)
if validate.has_flag(NodeFlag.RETRYABLE):
    ...
```

## Flag Reference

### Execution Control

| Flag | Engine Behavior |
|------|----------------|
| `ENTRY` | Marks the starting node. Set via `is_entry=True`. Read by `PromptGraph(nodes=[...])` (the first such node becomes the entry) and by `from_pool()` / `build_agent(node_pool=...)` (the pool's first step). A node added later with `add_node()` needs `set_entry()`. |
| `TERMINAL` | Set via `is_terminal=True`. Only an `AutonomousNode` pool reads it: a terminal step that succeeds ends the autonomous loop and writes the answer. In a static graph it does nothing; end a path with `default_next="__end__"` or an edge to `"__end__"`. |
| `CRITICAL` | If this node errors, the engine **aborts the run** right away: post-node hooks, mutations and transitions are skipped, the stream gets `on_node_error` with `critical: True`, `ExecutionReport.error` is set, and `ainvoke()` raises `GraphExecutionError` (the node's exception is its `__cause__`). |
| `SKIP_ON_ERROR` | If the **previous** node's result has an `error` (including a note a hook wrote, such as a `TimingHook` overrun), this node does not run: its result is empty with `transition_reason="skipped_on_error"`, and the transitions are resolved from that. Useful for optional enrichment steps. |
| `RETRYABLE` | On failure (a result with an `error`, or an exception), the engine runs the node again, up to `max_iterations` attempts in total (default 10), waiting `min(0.5 * 2**n, 8)` seconds between attempts (0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 8s...). Before each retry `state.context["_retry_attempt"]` and `["_retry_error"]` are set, so the node can adapt; both are removed afterwards. The attempts run through `execute()`, so a streamed run gets no token chunks from a `RETRYABLE` node. A [`RetryNode`](engine-nodes.md#retrynode) is never retried this way (it retries itself). |
| `REQUIRES_HUMAN` | Sets `state.context["_awaiting_human"]` to the node name and awaits `on_human_required(node_name, state)` on every hook that has it, before the node runs. The node still executes; the flag does not pause anything by itself. An exception in `on_human_required` is logged and the run goes on (before 1.7.0 it ended the run). For a real approval step, use [`HumanNode`](engine-nodes.md#humannode). |

### Context & Memory

| Flag | Engine Behavior |
|------|----------------|
| `NO_HISTORY` | Before the node runs, the engine keeps only the first message when it is a system message (no messages otherwise). Afterwards the original messages are restored, plus the messages the node added. The node then sees no user question, so give it what it needs through `input_keys` or `inherit_context_from`. |
| `ISOLATED_CONTEXT` | The node runs with a `state.context` holding only its `input_keys` (empty when it has none). Afterwards the original context is restored, and only the node's `output_key` and `{name}_output` values are merged back. |
| `CACHEABLE` | Within one run, a second visit to the node with the same `input_keys` values returns the first visit's result (output, raw output and `next_node`; no new messages or tool calls) without executing. The key is the node name plus the `input_keys` values (only the name for a node without `input_keys`). The cache lives in `state.context["_node_cache"]`, holds up to 128 results, skips results with an error, and starts empty on every run, so it never carries results between runs. |

### Model Selection

| Flag | Engine Behavior |
|------|----------------|
| `INJECT_TOOLS` | A `PromptNode` receives the engine's tools at runtime (the tools `build_agent()` discovered, or `PromptGraphEngine(tools=...)`) on top of its own. Set via `inject_tools=True`. Other node types ignore it. |
| `LIGHTWEIGHT` | If the node has no `model_override` and the engine was created with a `lightweight_model`, the engine swaps to that model for this node. `build_agent` creates the engine without one, so in an agent the flag has no effect; use `model_override` there. `ThinkNode` has this flag by default. |

### Observability

| Flag | Engine Behavior |
|------|----------------|
| `OBSERVABLE` | After the node runs, awaits `on_observable_event(event, state)` on every hook that has it, with a `NodeEvent(event="on_node_metrics", data={node_name, duration_ms, total_tokens, tool_calls, error})`. `duration_ms` is the node's own measurement (the engine's timing is set afterwards). An exception in the hook is logged and the run goes on (before 1.7.0 it ended the run). |
| `VERBOSE` | Logs the first 2,000 characters of the raw output at DEBUG level on the `promptise.engine` logger. |

### Output Processing

| Flag | Engine Behavior |
|------|----------------|
| `SUMMARIZE_OUTPUT` | If `raw_output` is longer than 1,000 characters, the engine makes one extra model call (the engine's model) to summarize it and replaces `NodeResult.raw_output` with the summary. The conversation, `output` and `state.context["{name}_output"]` keep the full text, so it mainly shortens what hooks and reports see. A failed summary call is logged and ignored. |
| `VALIDATE_OUTPUT` | Validates `result.output` against the node's `output_schema` (a Pydantic model, or a dict whose keys must be present). Problems are added to `result.guards_failed` (an `on_guard_fail` edge can route on them); a pass adds `"output_schema_validation"` to `guards_passed`. Does nothing without an `output_schema` or with a `None` output. |

### Concurrency & State

| Flag | Engine Behavior |
|------|----------------|
| `READONLY` | Declares that this node only reads state. Informational: the engine does not act on it (hooks and your own code can, with `node.has_flag()`). |
| `STATEFUL` | Declares that this node writes `state.context`. Informational. |
| `PARALLEL_SAFE` | Declares that this node can run concurrently. Informational: `ParallelNode` and `FanOutNode` run their children concurrently whatever their flags. |

## Pre-built Reasoning Node Flags

Each reasoning node ships with sensible default flags:

| Node | Default Flags | Rationale |
|------|--------------|-----------|
| ThinkNode | `READONLY`, `LIGHTWEIGHT` | Pure reasoning, no state writes, smaller model sufficient |
| ReflectNode | `STATEFUL`, `OBSERVABLE` | Writes reflections to state, worth logging |
| ObserveNode | `STATEFUL` | Writes entities/facts to state.context |
| JustifyNode | `READONLY`, `OBSERVABLE`, `VERBOSE` | Audit trail, full logging matters |
| CritiqueNode | `READONLY`, `OBSERVABLE` | Pure analysis, severity worth logging |
| PlanNode | `STATEFUL`, `OBSERVABLE` | Writes to state.plan |
| SynthesizeNode | `OBSERVABLE` | Final output, important to capture |
| ValidateNode | `READONLY`, `VALIDATE_OUTPUT` | Quality gate, validates own output |
| RetryNode | none | Retries itself; the engine does not retry it again |
| FanOutNode | `PARALLEL_SAFE` | Designed for concurrent execution |

## Custom Flags

The flag set accepts any hashable value. You can define domain-specific flags:

```python
class MyFlags:
    AUDIT_REQUIRED = "audit_required"
    PII_SENSITIVE = "pii_sensitive"

PromptNode("handle_user_data",
    flags={MyFlags.PII_SENSITIVE, NodeFlag.OBSERVABLE},
)

# Check in hooks
class AuditHook:
    async def post_node(self, node, result, state):
        if node.has_flag(MyFlags.AUDIT_REQUIRED):
            await audit_log.record(node.name, result)
        return result
```

## Engine Configuration

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraphEngine

engine = PromptGraphEngine(
    graph=graph,
    model=main_model,
    lightweight_model=small_model,  # Used for LIGHTWEIGHT nodes
)
```

Flags are processed in this order around a node: `SKIP_ON_ERROR`, `CACHEABLE`
(lookup), `NO_HISTORY`, `ISOLATED_CONTEXT`, `LIGHTWEIGHT`, `REQUIRES_HUMAN`;
then the node runs (with `RETRYABLE` retries); then the restores, `CACHEABLE`
(store), `VERBOSE`, `OBSERVABLE`, `SUMMARIZE_OUTPUT`, `VALIDATE_OUTPUT`;
then `CRITICAL`. A skipped or cached node gets none of the post-execute steps.

================================================================================
Page: Prebuilt Reasoning Graph Factories
URL: https://docs.promptise.com/core/engine-prebuilts/
================================================================================

# Prebuilt Reasoning Patterns

Ten ready-to-use reasoning patterns: nine you can name with `build_agent(agent_pattern="...")` and `PromptGraph.pipeline(...)`, which takes your nodes. Each factory is a static method on `PromptGraph` that returns a configured graph; pass it as `agent_pattern` to `build_agent()` or run it with `PromptGraphEngine`.

With a pattern name, `build_agent` passes its tools, its system prompt (`instructions`) and `graph_blocks` to the factory (for `research`, the tools become `search_tools`; for `code-action`, the `code_action=` settings and a sandbox factory are added). With no `agent_pattern` at all, the default ReAct graph gets the tools, the system prompt and `graph_blocks` too (before 1.7.0 it did not get `graph_blocks`). An unknown name raises `ValueError`.

!!! note "Node budgets"
    Each node runs at most its own `max_iterations` times per run. Under
    `build_agent`, the `reason` node of `react` (and of the default graph) and
    of `managed` gets `max_agent_iterations` (default 25) as its budget, so `N`
    allows `N` model calls; the other patterns keep the budgets their factories
    set, within the run's cap of `max_agent_iterations` node executions.
    `PromptGraphEngine` applies no engine-wide per-node ceiling unless you pass
    `max_node_iterations=` (before 1.7.0 it capped every node at 25, so
    `managed`'s 30 ran as 25).

## ReAct (Default)

Single PromptNode with tools. The LLM decides when to call tools and when to answer.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[reason] -->|tool calls| A
    A -->|final answer| END[__end__]

    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", servers=my_servers)
# or explicitly:
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="react")
```

The engine loops: LLM → tools → LLM → tools → ... → final answer.

```python
PromptGraph.react(
    tools=None,              # Tools (@tool functions, MCP tools)
    system_prompt="",        # The reason node's instructions
    blocks=None,             # PromptBlock objects
    max_node_iterations=15,  # The reason node's max_iterations (each model call counts)
)
```

One `PromptNode("reason")` with `context_scope="auto"` and `default_next="__end__"`.

## Verify (single-pass self-checking)

A single LLM call in which the model must **plan, solve, and verify its own
answer** before responding. It adds the accuracy benefit of an explicit
self-verification step at **one-turn latency**, no multi-call overhead.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["reason<br/>(plan → solve → verify)"] --> END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="verify")
```

```python
PromptGraph.verify(
    tools=None,
    system_prompt="",
    blocks=None,
    max_node_iterations=6,
)
```

One `PromptNode("reason")` whose instructions add a PLAN, SOLVE, VERIFY,
final-answer structure after `system_prompt`. It has `context_scope="full"`
(no compaction) and a budget of 6 model calls.

!!! note "When it helps"
    The self-check is part of the same generation, so it costs output tokens,
    not extra calls. It is most useful where a single pass makes careless
    errors; a model that already reasons carefully may gain little over a
    direct prompt. Measure it on your own tasks. For multi-stage deliberate
    reasoning with per-stage context scoping, compose a custom graph (see
    *Custom Graph*).

## Managed (context-managed tool loop)

For **deep multi-tool tasks**, traversing a database or graph, gathering
many facts then aggregating. A single tool-using node run with
`context_scope="ledger"`: instead of feeding the model an ever-growing
transcript of tool calls and results (where it loses track and re-queries the
same facts), each turn it sees the task, its most recent exchange, and a
compact **deduplicated "facts gathered" ledger**. A call the model does
repeat runs the tool again (its result may have changed); to answer repeats
of lookups whose result cannot change from the earlier result, opt those
tools in with `context_compaction=ContextCompaction(reuse_results=[...])`
(see [Repeated calls run the tool](../guides/context-lifecycle.md#repeated-calls-run-the-tool)).

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["reason<br/>(tool loop + facts ledger)"] --> END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="managed")
```

```python
PromptGraph.managed(
    tools=my_tools,
    system_prompt="",
    blocks=None,
    max_node_iterations=30,   # deep tasks make many calls (max_agent_iterations under build_agent)
)
```

The underlying primitive is [`PromptNode(context_scope="ledger")`](engine-nodes.md#context-scope),
which any custom graph can use on a long-running tool node.

!!! note "What it does, honestly"
    The ledger **bounds context** on long tool chains: the request stops
    growing with every tool result. Whether it also cuts tool calls depends
    on the model: models that re-query facts buried in a long transcript make
    fewer calls with it, others re-read facts the ledger lists. A result the
    model fetches again is kept in full from then on, so it does not have to
    re-read it a third time. Measure your own model with
    `ContextCompaction(enabled=False)` as the baseline. It is an
    **efficiency** primitive: it does not by itself make the model's final
    answer more correct.

## Code-Action (one sandboxed program)

For **aggregation / data-traversal tasks**, the model writes **one Python
program** over your tools in a single LLM turn, instead of chaining dozens of
conversational tool calls. The program runs in Promptise's hardened Docker
sandbox; its tool calls bridge back to the real host tools, so the model gets
code's exactness (loops, sums, filters, joins) while every tool call still
keeps its protections, approval gates if configured, plus budget/health/audit
hooks when the Agent Runtime has attached them, and the node enforces a hard
`max_tool_calls` cap on each program regardless.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["reason<br/>(write 1 program)"] --> S["run in sandbox<br/>(tools bridged to host)"]
    S --> END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="code-action")  # sandbox auto-enabled

# Tune the pattern from build_agent (unknown keys are rejected):
agent = await build_agent(
    ...,
    agent_pattern="code-action",
    code_action={"exec_timeout": 60, "max_repairs": 2, "max_tool_calls": 20},
)
```

```python
PromptGraph.code_action(
    tools=my_tools,
    system_prompt="",
    blocks=None,
    sandbox_factory=...,   # injected by build_agent
    max_repairs=1,         # re-try once on a failed program, feeding the error back
    exec_timeout=120,      # max seconds the program may run
    max_tool_calls=50,     # hard cap on each program's tool calls
)
```

**The tool-call budget.** Every call a program makes counts against
`max_tool_calls`, failed ones included. Once a program reaches it, each further
call raises `ToolBudgetExceeded` in the program without running the tool, a
warning is logged, and the program's output is discarded (it is incomplete,
even if the program caught the error). The prompt says the cap exists but not
its value, and forbids skipping or truncating records to stay under it. After a
budget hit the repair asks for a program that does the whole job in fewer calls
(it gets a fresh budget, so a run makes at most `(max_repairs + 1) ×
max_tool_calls` calls), or for the reply `CANNOT_FINISH_WITHIN_CALL_CAP`. That
reply, or a budget hit with no repair left, fails the node, and the run raises
`CodeActionBudgetError` (a `GraphExecutionError`) rather than answering from
part of the data. MCP tool results that
are JSON text reach the program decoded (lists, dicts, numbers), and an MCP
tool error raises in the program. `ExecutionReport.tool_calls` counts the
programs' calls. See [Code-Action](../guides/code-action.md#the-tool-call-budget).

**The mechanism.** In one turn the model writes a program that calls your tools
as ordinary Python functions. Inside the sandbox those functions are RPC stubs:
each writes a request to the workspace; a concurrent host loop runs the *real*
tool and writes back the response. The sandbox has a **read-only rootfs, dropped
capabilities, and no network**, the program's only outside reach is your
bridged tools.

!!! warning "Requirements & honest scope"
    Requires **Docker** (auto-enabled for this pattern). It shines when your
    tools return **structured data** (lists/dicts/numbers) the program can use
    directly, and on tasks a conversational loop gets wrong by re-querying and
    mis-aggregating. It is a *pattern, not a replacement*, for ambiguous or
    conversational tasks prefer `react`/`managed`. `PromptGraph.code_action()`
    without a `sandbox_factory` builds a graph whose node fails with "code-action
    requires a sandbox"; `build_agent(agent_pattern="code-action")` supplies one.

## PEOATR

Plan → Act → Think → Reflect → Answer. Structured reasoning with specialized nodes.

```mermaid
graph TD
    P[plan] -->|quality < 3| P
    P --> A[act]
    A -->|tool calls| A
    A --> T[think]
    T -->|continue| A
    T -->|reflect| R[reflect]
    R -->|continue| A
    R -->|replan| P
    R -->|answer| ANS[answer]
    ANS --> END[__end__]

    style P fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style A fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style T fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style R fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style ANS fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="peoatr")
```

```python
PromptGraph.peoatr(
    tools=None,                    # Tools for the act node
    system_prompt="",              # Shared system prompt
    blocks=None,                   # Shared blocks
    planning_instructions="",     # Extra instructions for the plan node
    acting_instructions="",       # Extra instructions for the act node
    thinking_instructions="",     # Extra instructions for the think node
    reflecting_instructions="",   # Extra instructions for the reflect node
    max_act_steps=12,             # Act budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
)
```

Each stage has its own role:

- **Plan** (PlanNode): Create subgoals and rate the plan; a plan rated below 3 is redone
- **Act** (PromptNode): Execute tools for the active subgoal, then summarize what it found
- **Think** (ThinkNode): Analyze the results: call another tool now (`continue`) or step back (`reflect`)
- **Reflect** (ReflectNode): Evaluate progress and route: `answer`, `replan` or `continue`
- **Answer** (SynthesizeNode): Write the final answer from the gathered results

Plan, think and reflect return structured output (`PeoatrPlan`, `PeoatrThought`, `PeoatrReflection` in `promptise.engine.prebuilts`), so their routing decisions always reach the engine. Every stage has an iteration budget (plan 3, act and think `max_act_steps`, reflect 4). A stage that has used its budget hands over to `answer` (`plan` hands over to `act`), so a run always ends with a written answer instead of looping to the engine's step cap.

## Research

Search → Verify → Synthesize. Three-stage research pipeline with optional verification.

```mermaid
graph LR
    S[search] -->|tool calls| S
    S --> V[verify]
    V -->|pass| SY[synthesize]
    V -->|fail| S
    SY --> END[__end__]

    style S fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style V fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style SY fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="research")
```

```python
PromptGraph.research(
    search_tools=None,       # Tools for the search node
    synthesis_tools=None,    # Tools for the synthesize node (optional)
    system_prompt="",        # Shared system prompt
    blocks=None,             # Shared blocks
    verify=True,             # Include verification step (set False to skip)
    max_search_steps=12,     # Search budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
    max_verify_rounds=2,     # How many times verify may run
)
```

- **Search** (PromptNode): Gather information with the tools, then reply with the findings. After a failed check it sees the verifier's issues (`state.context["verification"]`) and looks up what is missing.
- **Verify** (ValidateNode): A model call that checks the findings against the tool results in the conversation and returns a `ResearchVerdict` (`passes`, `issues`; in `promptise.engine.prebuilts`): every claim backed by a tool result, nothing contradicting the sources or itself, the whole question covered. A failed check routes back to search.
- **Synthesize** (PromptNode): Write the final answer from the findings.

Verify runs at most `max_verify_rounds` times; once it has, and when search has used its budget, the run moves on to synthesize, so it always ends with a written answer. Each check is one extra model call; pass `verify=False` for search → synthesize without it. For a deterministic check without a model call instead, build the graph yourself with a [`GuardNode`](engine-nodes.md) and your own guards in place of verify.

## Autonomous

Agent receives a pool of configured nodes and dynamically decides which to execute at each step.

```mermaid
graph TD
    AU[AutonomousNode] -->|step 1| N1[reason]
    AU -->|step 2| N2[analyze]
    AU -->|step 3| N3[synthesize]
    AU -->|done| END[__end__]

    N1 -.->|result| AU
    N2 -.->|result| AU
    N3 -.->|result| AU

    style AU fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style N1 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N3 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="autonomous")
```

```python
PromptGraph.autonomous(
    node_pool=None,          # List of BaseNode instances to choose from
    system_prompt="",        # System prompt for the planner
    tools=None,              # Tools for the default reason node (if no pool provided)
    max_steps=15,            # Maximum autonomous decision steps
    blocks=None,             # PromptBlocks for the default nodes
    max_tool_rounds=10,      # Model calls per reason step in the default pool
)
```

The LLM sees the node catalog (names, descriptions, the tools each step calls, which steps finish the run) and picks the next step, or `__done__`. If no pool is provided, the default pool is `reason` (with the tools), `analyze` and `synthesize`, which writes the final answer and is terminal.

- **A step runs its whole tool loop.** A chosen node is re-run while its model keeps calling tools (up to the node's `max_iterations`), so one step can make several tool calls and read their results before the agent picks again.
- **The routing exchange stays out of the conversation.** The step menu and the model's JSON choice are sent for that one call and never added to the messages, so they can't pile up or become the reply.
- **Tool names map to steps.** A tool name given as the next step runs the pool node that has that tool; an unknown name is reported back to the next routing call.
- **The run ends with an answer.** When the agent finishes (`__done__`, `max_steps`, or an unparseable choice) without a terminal node having run last, the `AutonomousNode`'s `answer_node` runs, by default the first terminal node; with none in the pool, the node asks the model for the final answer itself.
- **Streaming.** `AutonomousNode` streams the chosen steps' model chunks and tool events; the routing calls are not streamed.

## Deliberate

Think → Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Answer. Slower, higher-quality reasoning that thinks before acting and observes results carefully.

```mermaid
graph TD
    TH[think] --> PL[plan]
    PL -->|quality < 3| PL
    PL --> AC[act]
    AC -->|tool calls| AC
    AC --> OB[observe]
    OB --> RE[reflect]
    RE -->|continue| AC
    RE -->|replan| PL
    RE -->|answer| ANS[answer]
    ANS --> END[__end__]

    style TH fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style PL fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style AC fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style OB fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style RE fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style ANS fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="deliberate")
```

```python
PromptGraph.deliberate(
    tools=None,              # Tools for the act node
    system_prompt="",        # Shared system prompt
    blocks=None,             # Shared blocks
    max_act_steps=12,        # Act budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
)
```

Uses reasoning nodes: ThinkNode → PlanNode → PromptNode (with tools) → ObserveNode → ReflectNode → SynthesizeNode. Plan and reflect return structured output (`PeoatrPlan`, `PeoatrReflection`, as in PEOATR), so the plan's quality gate and reflect's `continue` / `replan` / `answer` route always reach the engine. Every stage has a budget (plan 3, act `max_act_steps`, reflect 4); act and reflect hand over to `answer` when theirs is used, so the run always ends with the `answer` stage's written reply.

## Debate

Adversarial debate. The proposer answers with tools, the critic and the judge send it back until the answer holds up, then `answer` writes the reply.

```mermaid
graph TD
    PR[proposer] -->|tool calls| PR
    PR --> CR[critic]
    CR -->|severity high| PR
    CR -->|severity low| JU[judge]
    JU -->|fail| PR
    JU -->|pass| ANS[answer]
    ANS --> END[__end__]

    style PR fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style CR fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style JU fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style ANS fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="debate")  # the proposer gets the agent's tools
```

```python
PromptGraph.debate(
    system_prompt="",        # Shared system prompt
    tools=None,              # Tools for the proposer
    blocks=None,             # Shared blocks
    max_rounds=3,            # How many times the critic and the judge may each run
    max_proposer_steps=12,   # Proposer budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
)
```

- **Proposer** (PromptNode): Answers with the tools. On a revision it sees the latest critique and verdict (`state.context["critique"]`, `state.context["verdict"]`).
- **Critic** (CritiqueNode): Returns a `DebateCritique` (`weaknesses`, `improvements`, `severity` from 0.0 to 1.0); above 0.3 the answer goes back to the proposer.
- **Judge** (ValidateNode): Returns a `DebateVerdict` (`passes`, `issues`); a failed verdict goes back to the proposer, a pass goes to `answer`.
- **Answer** (SynthesizeNode): Writes the final reply: the latest proposal, corrected for any issue still listed.

The schemas are in `promptise.engine.prebuilts`. When the critic has run `max_rounds` times the run goes to the judge; when the judge or the proposer has used its budget, it goes to `answer`, so a debate always ends with a written answer.

## Pipeline

Simple sequential pipeline. Chains provided nodes with always edges. No loops, no conditions.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[step 1] --> B[step 2] --> C[step 3] --> END[__end__]

    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode

graph = PromptGraph.pipeline(
    PromptNode("extract", instructions="Extract key facts."),
    PromptNode("analyze", instructions="Analyze the facts."),
    PromptNode("format", instructions="Format the results."),
)
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern=graph)
```

```python
PromptGraph.pipeline(
    PromptNode("extract"),   # Variadic: the nodes to chain, in order
    PromptNode("summarize"),
)
```

Automatically sets the first node as entry. The last node defaults to `__end__`.

## Custom Graph

Build any topology. Pass directly to `build_agent()`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    P[plan] --> S[search]
    S --> A[analyze]
    A -->|quality >= 4| W[write]
    A -->|quality < 4| S
    W --> R[review]
    R -->|approved| END[__end__]
    R -->|rejected| W

    style P fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style A fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style W fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style R fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
```

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode, GuardNode
from promptise.engine.skills import planner, web_researcher, summarizer
from promptise.prompts.guards import LengthGuard


class Analysis(BaseModel):
    findings: str
    quality: int   # 1-5: is the research good enough to write from?


graph = PromptGraph("custom", mode="static")
graph.add_node(planner("plan"))
graph.add_node(web_researcher("search", tools=search_tools))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("analyze", instructions="Analyze the findings and rate their quality 1-5.",
                          output_schema=Analysis, output_key="analysis", max_iterations=3,
                          transitions={"error": "write"}))
graph.add_node(summarizer("write", input_keys=["analysis"]))
graph.add_node(GuardNode("review", guards=[LengthGuard(max_length=2000)],
                         on_pass="__end__", on_fail="write"))

graph.always("plan", "search")
graph.always("search", "analyze")
graph.when("analyze", "write", lambda r: (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) >= 4)
graph.when("analyze", "search", lambda r: (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) < 4)
graph.always("write", "review")

graph.set_entry("plan")
assert graph.validate() == []
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern=graph)
```

!!! tip "Learn the concept"

    - [AI Agent Reasoning Patterns in Python: From ReAct to Debate](https://www.promptise.com/guides/view/ai-agent-reasoning-patterns) -- How the prebuilt patterns work and which one fits a task.
    - [Plan-and-Execute Agents in Python: Beyond the ReAct Loop](https://www.promptise.com/guides/view/plan-and-execute-agent-python) -- Plan, act, verify, reflect, explained on one task.

# Skills Library

Pre-configured node factories for common agent tasks, in `promptise.engine.skills`. Each function returns a node with task-specific instructions. Import them from `promptise.engine.skills` by name: `critic` in particular is also the name of a perspective in `promptise.prompts`.

```python
from promptise.engine.skills import critic, planner, web_researcher

nodes = [planner("plan", is_entry=True), web_researcher("search", tools=[]), critic("review")]
print([type(n).__name__ for n in nodes])   # ['PromptNode', 'PromptNode', 'CritiqueNode']
```

Every setting a skill picks (`instructions`, `tool_choice`, `tools`,
`default_next`, ...) is a default: pass the same keyword to override it, as
for any parameter of the node class. Before 1.7.0 the standard skills fixed
some of them, and passing one again raised `TypeError: got multiple values
for keyword argument`.

## Standard Skills

### web_researcher

Search the web with multi-source citation and fact verification.

```python
web_researcher(
    name="web_research",
    tools=None,              # Search tools (BaseTool instances)
    max_iterations=5,        # Model calls per run (each tool-loop round counts)
    **kwargs,                # Other PromptNode parameters
)
# Returns: PromptNode
```

### code_reviewer

Analyzes code for security vulnerabilities, performance issues, best practices, and logic errors.

```python
code_reviewer(
    name="code_review",
    tools=None,              # Code analysis tools
    **kwargs,                # All PromptNode parameters
)
# Returns: PromptNode
```

### data_analyst

Evidence-based analysis with data-backed claims and confidence levels.

```python
data_analyst(
    name="analyze",
    tools=None,              # Data query tools
    **kwargs,                # All PromptNode parameters
)
# Returns: PromptNode
```

### fact_checker

Validates findings for accuracy. Returns a GuardNode with pass/fail routing.

```python
fact_checker(
    name="verify",
    guards=None,             # Guard instances; None means no guards, so every check passes
    on_pass="__end__",       # Node on pass
    on_fail=None,            # Node on fail
    **kwargs,                # Other GuardNode parameters
)
# Returns: GuardNode (no model call; pass the guards that do the checking)
```

### summarizer

Compresses information into structured response: key finding, supporting details, sources.

```python
summarizer(
    name="summarize",
    max_length=2000,         # Length asked for in the instructions (chars); not enforced
    **kwargs,                # Other PromptNode parameters
)
# Returns: PromptNode with no tools and default_next="__end__"
```

### planner

Creates step-by-step plans with self-evaluation (rates quality 1-5).

```python
planner(
    name="plan",
    max_subgoals=4,          # Number of subgoals asked for in the instructions
    **kwargs,                # Other PromptNode parameters
)
# Returns: PromptNode (not a PlanNode: it does not set state.plan; use PlanNode for that)
```

### decision_router

Routes to next step based on progress. Lightweight LLM call to choose between named routes.

```python
decision_router(
    name="decide",
    routes=None,             # Dict mapping route labels to node names
    **kwargs,                # Other RouterNode parameters (default_next, model_override, ...)
)
# Returns: RouterNode
```

### formatter

Pure data transformation (no LLM call) for formatting final output.

```python
formatter(
    name="format",
    output_key="formatted_result",  # Where to store in state.context
    transform=None,                  # fn(state) -> Any; without one the node fails
    **kwargs,                        # Other TransformNode parameters
)
# Returns: TransformNode with default_next="__end__"
```

## Reasoning Skills

Pre-built reasoning node factories. Each returns the [reasoning node](engine-nodes.md#reasoning-nodes-pre-built-building-bricks) of the same kind, with its built-in instructions and default [Node Flags](engine-flags.md). Like the nodes themselves, they read routing and state fields only from a structured output, so pass an `output_schema` when the node should route or update state.

### thinker

Gap analysis and next-step reasoning. Default flags: `READONLY`, `LIGHTWEIGHT`.

```python
thinker(
    name="think",
    **kwargs,                # All ThinkNode parameters (focus_areas, etc.)
)
# Returns: ThinkNode
```

### reflector

Self-evaluation and mistake correction. Default flags: `STATEFUL`, `OBSERVABLE`.

```python
reflector(
    name="reflect",
    **kwargs,                # All ReflectNode parameters (review_depth, etc.)
)
# Returns: ReflectNode
```

### critic

Adversarial review with severity-based routing. Default flags: `READONLY`, `OBSERVABLE`.

```python
from promptise.engine.skills import critic

critic(
    name="critique",
    **kwargs,                # All CritiqueNode parameters (severity_threshold, etc.)
)
# Returns: CritiqueNode
```

### justifier

Chain-of-thought justification for audit trail. Default flags: `READONLY`, `OBSERVABLE`, `VERBOSE`.

```python
justifier(
    name="justify",
    **kwargs,                # All JustifyNode parameters
)
# Returns: JustifyNode
```

### synthesizer

Combines all gathered data into a final answer. Default flags: `OBSERVABLE`.

```python
synthesizer(
    name="synthesize",
    **kwargs,                # All SynthesizeNode parameters
)
# Returns: SynthesizeNode
```

### validator_node

LLM-powered quality gate with pass/fail routing. Default flags: `READONLY`, `VALIDATE_OUTPUT`.

```python
validator_node(
    name="validate",
    criteria=None,           # List of validation criteria strings
    **kwargs,                # All ValidateNode parameters (on_pass, on_fail, etc.)
)
# Returns: ValidateNode
```

### observer_node

## Usage

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph
from promptise.engine.skills import (
    planner, web_researcher, reflector, synthesizer,
)

graph = PromptGraph("research-team")
graph.add_node(planner("plan", is_entry=True))
graph.add_node(web_researcher("search", tools=search_tools))
graph.add_node(reflector("reflect"))
graph.add_node(synthesizer("conclude", is_terminal=True))
```

## Customization

Skills are functions that return nodes. Pass any parameter of the node class, including the ones the skill sets:

```python
from promptise.engine import NodeFlag, PromptGraph
from promptise.engine.skills import summarizer, thinker, web_researcher

graph = PromptGraph("custom")

# Custom max iterations
graph.add_node(web_researcher("search", tools=my_tools, max_iterations=10))

# Custom instructions
graph.add_node(summarizer("conclude", instructions="Summarize in bullet points only."))

# Reasoning skills take any parameter, including their instructions
graph.add_node(thinker("think", instructions="List what is still unknown."))

# Per-node model override
graph.add_node(thinker("think_fast", model_override="openai:gpt-5-mini"))

# Additional flags
graph.add_node(web_researcher("search",
    tools=my_tools,
    flags={NodeFlag.CRITICAL, NodeFlag.RETRYABLE},
))
```

# Path-Scoped Skill Activation

Register reasoning-graph skills with glob patterns so they only activate when the agent is working in a matching directory. A TypeScript review skill stays hidden when the agent operates in a Python repo.

```python
from promptise.engine import Skill, SkillRegistry
from promptise.engine.skills import code_reviewer

reg = SkillRegistry()
reg.register(
    Skill(
        name="ts-reviewer",
        description="Reviews TypeScript / React code.",
        paths=["**/*.tsx", "**/*.ts"],
        factory=lambda **kw: code_reviewer("ts_review", **kw),
    )
)

# Only activates when cwd contains .tsx or .ts files
active = reg.activate_for(cwd=".")
```

---

## Why path scoping?

Modern agents have many skills (web research, code review, data analysis, summarization, etc.). Including all of them in every prompt wastes tokens and confuses the LLM. Path scoping is a cheap, declarative way to keep the active set small and contextual, no code changes needed when the agent moves between projects.

---

## Skill dataclass

```python
@dataclass
class Skill:
    name: str                          # unique identifier
    description: str = ""              # shown to the agent
    paths: list[str] = []             # glob patterns, empty = always active
    factory: Callable[..., Any] = None # returns a node, tool, or any effect
    metadata: dict[str, Any] = {}     # extra frontmatter fields
```

`matches_cwd(cwd)` returns `True` if any file under `cwd` matches any of the globs: first `Path(cwd).glob(pattern)` (so `**/*.ts` searches subdirectories), then `fnmatch` on every path relative to `cwd`, where `*` also matches `/`, so `*.ts` finds `src/app.ts` too. The walk stops at the first match, but a tree with no match is walked in full. Before 1.7.0 the `fnmatch` pass stopped after the first entry, so `*.ts` in practice matched the top level only. Empty `paths` = always active (global skill). A `cwd` that is not a directory matches nothing.

`create(**kwargs)` calls `factory(**kwargs)` and returns what it returns; a skill without a factory raises `ValueError`.

---

## SkillRegistry

| Method | Returns | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `register(skill)` | `None` | Add a skill; a name that is already registered raises `ValueError` |
| `unregister(name)` | `bool` | Remove by name; `False` when it was not registered |
| `get(name)` | `Skill \| None` | Look up by name |
| `all()` | `list[Skill]` | Every registered skill, in registration order |
| `activate_for(cwd=".")` | `list[Skill]` | The skills whose `paths` match under `cwd` (or are empty) |
| `names_active_for(cwd=".")` | `list[str]` | Their names, sorted |
| `load_directory(directory)` | `int` | Load skill files (below); returns how many were registered |
| `len(reg)`, `"name" in reg` | | Count and membership |

The registry holds no execution state, so one instance can be shared by several agents.

---

## File-based loading with frontmatter

Write a `.py` file that **starts** with a YAML-ish docstring header and defines a `create()` function. The header must be the first thing in the file: a comment, an import or `from __future__` above it means the file is not read as a skill.

```python title="skills/ts_review.py"
"""
name: ts-reviewer
description: Reviews TypeScript / React code.
paths:
  - src/**/*.tsx
  - src/**/*.ts
"""

def create(**kwargs):
    from promptise.engine.skills import code_reviewer
    return code_reviewer("ts_review", **kwargs)
```

Load an entire directory:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from promptise.engine import SkillRegistry

skills_dir = Path("skills")
skills_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(skills_dir / "ts_review.py").write_text('''"""
name: ts-reviewer
description: Reviews TypeScript / React code.
paths:
  - src/**/*.tsx
  - src/**/*.ts
"""


def create(**kwargs):
    from promptise.engine.skills import code_reviewer
    return code_reviewer("ts_review", **kwargs)
''')

reg = SkillRegistry()
loaded = reg.load_directory(skills_dir)
print(f"Loaded {loaded} skills")                 # Loaded 1 skills
print(reg.names_active_for(cwd="."))             # [] until the cwd has src/**/*.ts files
```

How `load_directory()` treats files:

- Only `*.py` files directly in the directory (no subdirectories), in name order. A missing directory raises `FileNotFoundError`.
- A file without a recognizable header is skipped silently (it is not a skill file).
- The file is imported to get `create`, so **its code runs**: load only directories you trust. A file that fails to import or has no callable `create` is logged and skipped; so is a name that is already registered.
- `name` defaults to the file name without `.py`; a single `paths` string becomes a one-item list.

The frontmatter parser is built in, so no YAML library is needed. It recognizes `name`, `description`, `paths` (as a list), and passes any extra keys through as `metadata`. Scalars are converted: `true`/`yes`/`on`, `false`/`no`/`off`, `null`, integers and floats; quotes around a value are removed. Lines starting with `#` are ignored, and an empty line ends a list.

The same parser is public as `parse_frontmatter(source)`. It reads the first
triple-quoted docstring of a Python source string and returns its `key: value` lines
(and `- item` lists under a key) as a dict, or `None` when there is no docstring or
no recognizable key:

```python
from promptise.engine import parse_frontmatter

source = '''"""
name: ts-reviewer
description: Reviews TypeScript / React code.
paths:
  - src/**/*.tsx
  - src/**/*.ts
"""
'''
print(parse_frontmatter(source))
# {'name': 'ts-reviewer', 'description': 'Reviews TypeScript / React code.',
#  'paths': ['src/**/*.tsx', 'src/**/*.ts']}
print(parse_frontmatter("# a comment first\n" + source))   # None
```

---

## Using with PromptGraph

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, Skill, SkillRegistry
from promptise.engine.skills import summarizer

reg = SkillRegistry()
reg.register(Skill(name="summary", description="Summarize findings.",
                   factory=lambda **kw: summarizer("summarize", **kw)))   # no paths: always active

graph = PromptGraph("assistant")
for skill in reg.activate_for(cwd="."):
    graph.add_node(skill.create())
print(list(graph.nodes))   # ['summarize']
```

`activate_for()` checks the file system on every call, so call it when the
working directory changes (each run, or each project the agent switches to),
not once at startup.

# Building Custom Agentic Reasoning Patterns

This guide shows how to build your own agent reasoning strategies using the Reasoning Graph, from simple tool-calling agents to sophisticated multi-stage reasoning systems.

## Concepts

A **reasoning pattern** is a graph of nodes. Each node is a complete processing unit. The engine traverses the graph, executing nodes and following edges. The LLM decides the path at runtime.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Your Custom Pattern
        A[Node A<br/>plan] -->|route| B[Node B<br/>search]
        B -->|tool results| C[Node C<br/>analyze]
        C -->|quality OK| D[Node D<br/>respond]
        C -->|quality low| B
    end

    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style D fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
```

Each node controls:

- **What the LLM sees**: blocks, strategy, perspective, context layers
- **What the LLM can do**: tools, tool_choice, inject_tools
- **What the LLM must produce**: output_schema, guards
- **How data flows**: input_keys, output_key, inherit_context_from
- **Pre/post processing**: preprocessor, postprocessor
- **Where to go next**: transitions, default_next, LLM-routed

## Example 1: Simple Tool Agent

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[agent] -->|tool calls| A
    A -->|done| END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
```

The simplest pattern, one node with tools:

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode

graph = PromptGraph("simple-agent")
graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "agent",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Use tools to answer questions.",
    tools=my_tools,
    default_next="__end__",  # A tool-free answer ends the run
))
graph.set_entry("agent")
```

The engine handles everything: LLM calls, tool execution, re-entry, termination. After a turn with tool calls the engine re-enters the node on its own, so `default_next` only decides what happens after the final answer.

## Example 2: Research Pipeline

```mermaid
graph LR
    S[search<br/>inject_tools] -->|output_key| A[analyze<br/>inherit from search]
    A -->|output_key| W[write<br/>input_keys]
    W --> END[__end__]
    style S fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style A fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style W fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
```

Three stages with data flow between nodes:

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode
from promptise.prompts import chain_of_thought

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Analysis(BaseModel):
    key_findings: list[str]
    open_questions: list[str]


graph = PromptGraph("researcher", mode="static")

# Stage 1: Search (has tools). Its final reply text lands in state.context["search_output"].
graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "search",
    instructions="Search for information about the topic, then summarize what you found.",
    tools=search_tools,
    default_next="analyze",
))

# Stage 2: Analyze (reads the search summary, no tools, structured output)
graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "analyze",
    instructions="Analyze the search results. Identify key findings.",
    inherit_context_from="search",    # Reads state.context["search_output"]
    output_schema=Analysis,
    output_key="analysis",            # The parsed Analysis dict
    default_next="write",
))

# Stage 3: Write (reads the analysis, produces the final answer)
graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "write",
    instructions="Write a comprehensive answer based on the analysis.",
    input_keys=["analysis"],
    strategy=chain_of_thought,
    default_next="__end__",
))

graph.set_entry("search")
```

`output_key` holds the node's output: the parsed `Analysis` dict here, the
reply text for a plain-text node. `inherit_context_from` reads the other
side, `state.context["{name}_output"]`, which every `PromptNode` writes (its
reply text, or its structured output as JSON).

## Example 3: Quality-Controlled Output

```mermaid
graph TD
    D[draft] --> R{review<br/>GuardNode}
    R -->|pass| END[__end__]
    R -->|fail| REV[revise]
    REV --> R
    style D fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style REV fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
```

Add a guard node for quality control with retry:

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptNode, GuardNode, PromptGraph
from promptise.prompts.guards import ContentFilterGuard, LengthGuard

graph = PromptGraph("quality-agent", mode="static")

graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "draft",
    instructions="Write a technical blog post about the topic, with an introduction and a conclusion.",
    tools=research_tools,
    default_next="review",
))

# No model call: checks the last message (the latest draft) and routes.
graph.add_node(GuardNode(
    "review",
    guards=[
        LengthGuard(min_length=500, max_length=3000),
        ContentFilterGuard(required=["conclusion", "introduction"]),
    ],
    on_pass="__end__",
    on_fail="revise",
))

graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "revise",
    instructions=("The draft failed review: it must be 500-3000 characters and contain the "
                  "words 'introduction' and 'conclusion'. Rewrite it."),
    inherit_context_from="draft",
    default_next="review",
    max_iterations=3,                # at most 3 revisions,
    transitions={"error": "__end__"},  # then stop with the last draft
))

graph.set_entry("draft")
```

`GuardNode` does not write the guard messages anywhere the model reads, so put
the rules in the reviser's instructions (or read
`state.node_history[-1].guards_failed` in a custom node). The run ends on the
last message, so the reply is the latest draft.

## Example 4: Parallel Research

```mermaid
graph TD
    G[gather<br/>ParallelNode] --> SY[synthesize]
    SY --> END[__end__]
    subgraph Parallel
        W[web search]
        D[doc search]
        C[code search]
    end
    G --- W
    G --- D
    G --- C
    style G fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style SY fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
```

Search multiple sources simultaneously. Each child runs one model call: a
child that calls a tool runs it, but does not get a second turn to read the
result. The successful tool results go to `state.observations`, and
`synthesize` (a node without tools) sees the latest five in its prompt:

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptNode, ParallelNode, PromptGraph
from promptise.prompts import chain_of_thought, self_critique

graph = PromptGraph("parallel-research", mode="static")

graph.add_node(ParallelNode(
    "gather",
    nodes=[
        PromptNode("web", tools=[web_search], instructions="Search the web."),
        PromptNode("docs", tools=[doc_search], instructions="Search documentation."),
        PromptNode("code", tools=[code_search], instructions="Search codebases."),
    ],
    default_next="synthesize",
))

graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "synthesize",
    instructions="Combine findings from all three sources.",
    include_observations=True,
    strategy=chain_of_thought + self_critique,
    default_next="__end__",
))

graph.set_entry("gather")
```

## Example 5: Dynamic LLM Routing

```mermaid
graph TD
    T[triage] -->|route: simple| END[__end__]
    T -->|route: research| DR[deep research]
    T -->|route: code| CA[code agent]
    T -->|route: creative| CR[creative agent]
    DR --> END
    CA --> END
    CR --> END
    style T fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style DR fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style CA fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style CR fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
```

The LLM decides where to go at each step. Give the node an `output_schema` with a `route` field: the engine follows the transition whose key the model picks (a node name works too). Without a schema the reply is plain text and the route is never read.

```python
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode
from promptise.prompts import creative


class Triage(BaseModel):
    route: Literal["simple_answer", "research", "code_task", "creative"]


graph = PromptGraph("dynamic-agent", mode="static")

graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "triage",
    instructions="Analyze the user's request and decide the approach.",
    output_schema=Triage,
    transitions={
        "simple_answer": "__end__",
        "research": "deep_research",
        "code_task": "code_agent",
        "creative": "creative_agent",
    },
))

graph.add_node(PromptNode("deep_research", tools=search_tools, default_next="__end__"))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("code_agent", tools=code_tools, default_next="__end__"))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("creative_agent", perspective=creative, default_next="__end__"))

graph.set_entry("triage")
```

## Example 6: Custom Preprocessing

Transform data before the LLM sees it:

```python
from datetime import datetime


async def load_customer_data(state, config):
    """Preprocessor: load customer data into context."""
    customer_id = state.context.get("customer_id")
    if customer_id:
        data = await crm.get_customer(customer_id)
        state.context["customer_name"] = data.name
        state.context["customer_tier"] = data.tier
        state.context["customer_history"] = data.recent_tickets[:5]

async def format_ticket(output, state, config):
    """Postprocessor: format the reply as a support ticket."""
    return {
        "ticket_id": generate_id(),
        "customer": state.context.get("customer_name"),
        # output is the reply text (also in state.context["support_output"])
        "resolution": output,
        "created_at": datetime.now().isoformat(),
    }

graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "support",
    instructions="Resolve the customer's issue.",
    tools=support_tools,
    preprocessor=load_customer_data,
    postprocessor=format_ticket,
    output_key="ticket",
    default_next="__end__",
))
```

## Example 7: Custom Node Type

Build a completely custom node:

```python
from promptise.engine import BaseNode, GraphState, NodeResult

class APICallNode(BaseNode):
    """A node that calls an external API and processes the response."""

    def __init__(self, name, *, endpoint, headers=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(name, **kwargs)
        self.endpoint = endpoint
        self.headers = headers or {}

    async def execute(self, state, config):
        import httpx

        params = {k: state.context[k] for k in state.context if not k.startswith("_")}

        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            resp = await client.get(self.endpoint, params=params, headers=self.headers)
            data = resp.json()

        state.context[f"{self.name}_result"] = data
        state.observations.append({"tool": self.name, "result": str(data)[:500], "success": True})

        return NodeResult(node_name=self.name, node_type="api_call", output=data)

# Use it in a graph
graph.add_node(APICallNode("weather", endpoint="https://api.weather.com/current"))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("respond", inherit_context_from="weather"))
graph.always("weather", "respond")
```

## Example 8: Using the Graph with build_agent

```python
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Identity, Rules

# Build your custom graph
graph = PromptGraph("my-agent")
graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "main",
    blocks=[
        Identity("Senior data analyst"),
        Rules(["Always cite sources", "Include confidence levels"]),
    ],
    inject_tools=True,  # Receives the tools build_agent discovers
    default_next="__end__",
))
graph.set_entry("main")

# Pass it to build_agent: nodes with inject_tools=True get the MCP tools
agent = await build_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    servers={"analytics": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    agent_pattern=graph,
)

result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Analyze Q4 trends"}]})
```

## Debugging

### Graph Visualization

```python
print(graph.describe())
print(graph.to_mermaid())
```

### Validate before you run

```python
problems = graph.validate()   # [] when the entry, edges and transitions all resolve
assert not problems, problems
```

### Execution Report

```python
from promptise import resolve_model
from promptise.engine import PromptGraphEngine

engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph, resolve_model("openai:gpt-5-mini"))
result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Analyze Q4 trends"}]})
print(engine.last_report.summary())
```

### Step-by-Step Inspection

A `post_node` hook sees every node's `NodeResult` as the run goes:

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraphEngine


class PrintSteps:
    async def post_node(self, node, result, state):
        print(f"{result.node_name}: {result.duration_ms:.0f}ms, tokens={result.total_tokens}, "
              f"tools={len(result.tool_calls)}")
        return result


engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph=graph, model=model, hooks=[PrintSteps()])
result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Analyze Q4 trends"}]})
```

### Hooks for Debugging

```python
from promptise.engine import LoggingHook

engine = PromptGraphEngine(
    graph=graph,
    model=model,
    hooks=[LoggingHook()],  # Logs every node entry/exit
)
```

## Production Hardening

### Node Flags for Safety

Use [typed flags](../core/engine-flags.md) to make graphs production-safe:

```python
from promptise.engine import NodeFlag, PromptGraph, PromptNode
from promptise.engine.reasoning_nodes import ThinkNode, SynthesizeNode

graph = PromptGraph("production-safe", nodes=[
    # Must succeed: abort graph on failure
    ThinkNode("plan", is_entry=True, flags={NodeFlag.CRITICAL}),

    # Retry a failed model call with exponential backoff (up to max_iterations attempts)
    PromptNode("fetch_data", inject_tools=True, max_iterations=3,
               flags={NodeFlag.RETRYABLE, NodeFlag.OBSERVABLE}),

    # Skip enrichment if fetch failed: don't block the pipeline
    PromptNode("enrich", flags={NodeFlag.SKIP_ON_ERROR}),

    # Cache within the run: a revisit with the same input_keys values reuses the result
    PromptNode("analyze", flags={NodeFlag.CACHEABLE},
               input_keys=["data"]),

    # Final answer with a smaller model
    SynthesizeNode("answer", is_terminal=True,
                   model_override="openai:gpt-5-mini"),
])
```

### Processors for Data Quality

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine import PromptNode
from promptise.engine.processors import (
    chain_postprocessors, chain_preprocessors, context_enricher, json_extractor,
    state_summarizer, state_writer,
)


class Report(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    confidence: float
    sources: list[str]


PromptNode("analyze",
    output_schema=Report,
    input_keys=["data"],
    # Before the LLM call: cap long context values, add timestamp/iteration
    preprocessor=chain_preprocessors(
        state_summarizer(max_context_chars=4000),
        context_enricher(),
    ),
    # After: keep the fields you need, copy the answer into state.context
    postprocessor=chain_postprocessors(
        json_extractor(keys=["answer", "sources"]),
        state_writer(fields={"answer": "final_answer"}),
    ),
)
```

A preprocessor that raises fails the node before the model is called, so a
validator such as `input_validator()` stops it; a postprocessor's exception is
logged and the output kept. See [Processors](../core/engine-processors.md).

### Budget and Metrics Hooks

```python
from promptise.engine import PromptGraphEngine, MetricsHook, BudgetHook

metrics = MetricsHook()
engine = PromptGraphEngine(
    graph=graph,
    model=model,
    hooks=[
        metrics,
        BudgetHook(max_tokens=50000, max_cost_usd=0.50),
    ],
)

result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Analyze Q4 trends"}]})

# Inspect per-node performance
for node_name, stats in metrics.summary().items():
    print(f"{node_name}: {stats['calls']} calls, "
          f"{stats['total_tokens']} tokens, "
          f"{stats['total_duration_ms']:.0f}ms")
```

### Error Handling

A run that ends on a failed node (a provider error, a CRITICAL node, a RETRYABLE node out of attempts) raises `GraphExecutionError`, which carries the run's report:

```python
from promptise.engine import GraphExecutionError

try:
    result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Analyze Q4 trends"}]})
except GraphExecutionError as exc:
    print(f"Graph failed at {exc.node_name}: {exc.error}")
    report = exc.report
else:
    report = engine.last_report

print(report.summary())  # path, tokens, tool calls, guards
```

An agent from `build_agent` raises the same exceptions from `agent.ainvoke()`;
the report of a failed agent run is `exc.report`.

## Best Practices

1. **Start simple**: Use `PromptGraph.react()` first. Add complexity only when needed.
2. **One responsibility per node**: Each node should do ONE thing well.
3. **Use output_key/input_keys**: Explicit data flow is easier to debug than implicit state.
4. **Set max_iterations**: Every node that can loop should have a limit.
5. **Add guards**: Validate output at key checkpoints, not just at the end.
6. **Use flags for safety**: `CRITICAL` for must-succeed nodes, `RETRYABLE` for flaky calls, `SKIP_ON_ERROR` for optional steps.
7. **Use hooks for cross-cutting concerns**: Logging, timing, metrics, budget enforcement.
8. **Test incrementally**: Test each node in isolation, then the graph.
9. **Use model_override for cost**: Cheap models for routing/classification, expensive for reasoning/synthesis.
10. **Cap everything**: Observations (capped at 50), reflections (capped at 5), node iterations, total iterations.
11. **Give routing nodes a schema**: `route`, pass/fail and severity are read from structured output only.
12. **Call `graph.validate()`** in a test, it catches typos in edge and transition targets before a run does.

!!! tip "Learn the concept"

    - [AI Agent Reasoning Patterns in Python: From ReAct to Debate](https://www.promptise.com/guides/view/ai-agent-reasoning-patterns) -- How the prebuilt reasoning patterns work and how to choose one.
    - [Plan-and-Execute Agents in Python: Beyond the ReAct Loop](https://www.promptise.com/guides/view/plan-and-execute-agent-python) -- A plan, act, verify, reflect graph compared with ReAct.

================================================================================
Page: Inject MCP Tools into Graph Nodes
URL: https://docs.promptise.com/core/engine-tools/

# Runtime Tool Injection

When you use `build_agent(servers=...)`, MCP tools are discovered at startup. For the default ReAct pattern, these tools are automatically available. For custom graphs, you control which nodes get tools.

## How It Works

1. `build_agent()` discovers tools from MCP servers (plus `extra_tools`, cross-agent and sandbox tools)
2. Tools are converted to LangChain `BaseTool` instances
3. `build_agent()` hands them to the engine: `PromptGraphEngine(graph, model, tools=discovered)`
4. Nodes with `inject_tools=True` receive those tools at runtime, together with every tool another node of the graph declares
5. Injected tools merge with the node's own `tools` (no duplicates, the node's own tool wins on a name clash)

Nodes without `inject_tools=True` see only their own `tools`. `agent.tool_names` lists what was discovered; it does not mean every node can call them.

Which node types use injected tools:

| Node | Tools it can call |
|------|-------------------|
| `PromptNode` (and the reasoning nodes) with `inject_tools=True` | Its own `tools` plus the engine's tools |
| `PromptNode` without it | Its own `tools` only |
| `ToolNode` | Its own `tools` only |
| `CodeActionNode` | Its own `tools`; with none, all of the engine's tools |
| `AutonomousNode` | None itself; each pool step uses its own rule above, and the step menu lists each step's tools |

With `build_agent(optimize_tools="semantic")`, a tool selector narrows the
tools *offered* on each model call to the relevant ones; a call to a tool that
was not offered on that step still runs, since every candidate stays callable.

## Usage

```python
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode

graph = PromptGraph("my-agent", mode="static")

# This node gets ALL MCP tools at runtime
graph.add_node(PromptNode("search",
    instructions="Search for information.",
    inject_tools=True,
))

# This node gets NO tools (pure reasoning)
graph.add_node(PromptNode("think",
    instructions="Analyze the results.",
    inject_tools=False,
))

# This node gets ONLY its explicit tools + MCP tools
graph.add_node(PromptNode("enhanced",
    tools=[my_custom_calculator],
    inject_tools=True,   # MCP tools ALSO added
))

graph.always("search", "think")
graph.always("think", "__end__")
graph.set_entry("search")

agent = await build_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    servers={"tools": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    agent_pattern=graph,
)
```

## When to Use

| Scenario | `inject_tools` | Why |
|----------|---------------|-----|
| Tool-calling node | `True` | Needs MCP tools to do work |
| Pure reasoning | `False` | No tools, just thinking |
| Routing decision | `False` | Lightweight, no tool overhead |
| Guard/validation | `False` | No LLM call, no tools needed |
| Mixed (custom + MCP) | `True` + explicit `tools` | Both available |

## Without build_agent

Running a graph directly, pass the tools to the engine yourself:

```python
from promptise import resolve_model, tool
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptGraphEngine, PromptNode


@tool
def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Status of an order."""
    return f"Order {order_id}: shipped"


graph = PromptGraph("support", nodes=[
    PromptNode("answer", instructions="Answer with the tools.", inject_tools=True,
               is_entry=True, default_next="__end__"),
])
engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph, resolve_model("openai:gpt-5-mini"), tools=[lookup_order])
result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order A-17?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
```
